weeks.title: Jesus Calls Us Friends
weeks.theme: Jesus first became our friend, and that is how we learn to be a friend to others.
group: Read John 15:9-17. What is the difference between the “friends” and the “servants” Jesus speaks of?
When you make friends, do you value people more for being “useful” or for who they are?
Whom around you are you willing to befriend first this week, and what is one concrete way you will love your neighbor?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, invite a friend you rarely talk with deeply—a coworker, a neighbor, or someone on the edges of your church—to share a simple meal or a cup of coffee. Before you go, pray for them and ask the Lord to help you listen the way Jesus does. At the table, ask more and talk less, and remember one thing that weighs on their heart. When you get home, give thanks for this friendship, and keep praying about that concern throughout the coming week.

lessons.title: I Have Called You Friends
lessons.hear:
On the night of the Last Supper, Jesus said something to his disciples that changed everything: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

Imagine it: the Lord of the universe calling a group of fishermen, a tax collector, and some often-quarreling young men his “friends.” This wasn’t politeness; it was a promotion in identity. The difference between a servant and a friend is “knowing.” A servant only receives orders; a friend is let in on what’s in your heart. Jesus opened the Father’s heart to us—and that is friendship: being willing to let someone know the real you.

In this passage Jesus also models three marks of friendship. First, he takes the initiative and chooses: “You didn’t choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). Friendship doesn’t wait for the other person to come first; it reaches out first. Second, self-giving love: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). True friendship isn’t using each other; it is being willing to pay a price for the other. Third, bearing fruit together: friends don’t just kill time together; they live out life’s meaning together.

This week we will learn from Jesus how to be a friend. Many people find socializing exhausting because they are always trying to prove they deserve to be someone’s friend: they have to be fun, successful, useful. But the gospel reverses the order. Jesus called you his friend first—not because you performed well, but because he loves you. Someone who knows they have already been accepted by the best Friend of all no longer needs to people-please or compare. They can be at peace and go be a friend to others. So today, first be still, and let him tell you once again: “I have called you friend.”
lessons.light: Self-centered friendship asks, “What use is this person to me?” Selfless friendship asks, “How can I lay myself down for them?” Relationships matter more than things; people matter more than tasks. Jesus is my example: he chose first, opened his heart first, and laid down his life first—so our friendships also begin with going first.
think: In John 15:13-16, what are the marks of Jesus’ friendship?
Am I still using my performance to prove I am “worthy” of being someone’s friend?
Which friend can I open up to, or pay a small price for, today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling me your friend—not because I am good, but because you love me. I often wear myself out trying to prove myself to people, forgetting that you have already accepted me. Let me rest in your friendship, and make me like you: the first to reach out, the first to open my heart, willing to lay myself down for my friends. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write out John 15:15 and keep it on your phone or desk. Then message a friend you haven’t been in touch with for a long time and sincerely ask how they are doing.
lessons.quick: Once Jesus calls you friend, you no longer have to earn friendship by performing.
text: Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.
If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.
I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.
“This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.
Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.
You are my friends if you do whatever I command you.
No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.

You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you.
“I command these things to you, that you may love one another.

lessons.title: The Friend of Sinners
lessons.hear:
A brother working at a multinational company was very good at networking. Whoever could help him get promoted, he took out for coffee; whoever was of no use, he politely kept at arm’s length. At his company there was a coworker people often talked about behind his back—blunt, unpopular, always eating lunch alone. The brother thought, “Getting too close to him won’t do me any good.”

This is an old mindset we know well: friends should be people who are “useful,” “in my circle,” and “won’t embarrass me.” But what did people call Jesus? “A friend of tax collectors and sinners!” (Luke 7:34). It was meant as an insult, yet it became one of the gospel’s most beautiful titles.

Look at the story of Levi. Levi was a tax collector—in everyone’s eyes, a man who collected taxes for the Romans and often squeezed extra money out of his own people. Jesus walked past the tax office and said to him, “Follow me!” (Luke 5:27). Levi left everything to follow the Lord, and he even threw a great banquet for Jesus at his home, inviting many of his tax-collector friends. The religious leaders immediately grumbled: “Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?” (Luke 5:30). Jesus answered, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do” (Luke 5:31). He didn’t care about being labeled. He cared about the people others looked down on.

God’s perspective is this: friendship is not an investment but a channel of grace. When Jesus sat at the table with sinners, he wasn’t joining them in sin; he was like a doctor walking into a hospital ward, bringing people toward new life with love. Later, that brother was convicted by this passage and began having lunch with that coworker once a week. At first the coworker was guarded, but a few months later he said, “In this whole company, you’re the only one who asks me how my weekend was.” In that moment the brother realized he wasn’t doing a good deed—he was learning to be a friend the way Jesus is.
lessons.light: Networking thinking is self-centered socializing: treating people as rungs on a ladder. Jesus’ friendship is selfless: he moved toward the excluded and sat down at their tables. As we move from a worldly perspective to God’s perspective, we no longer see people by their usefulness, but by how precious they are in God’s eyes.
think: How did the Pharisees view Levi’s banquet, and how did Jesus respond?
In my circles, who is the person who “always eats lunch alone”?
What price am I willing to pay to befriend someone who is being left out?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the friend of tax collectors and sinners—and my friend too. I confess that I often choose friends by how useful they are and avoid people who might embarrass me. Give me your eyes to see the one who is left out, and give me courage to sit at their table and step into their life. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today at work, school, or church, find someone who is often alone, invite them to lunch or a cup of tea, and listen to them wholeheartedly.
lessons.quick: Jesus doesn’t choose friends by usefulness; he sits at the table of the despised.
text: After these things he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax office, and said to him, “Follow me!”
He left everything, and rose up and followed him.
Levi made a great feast for him in his house. There was a great crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining with them.
Their scribes and the Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus answered them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.”

lessons.title: Jesus Wept
lessons.hear:
Lazarus had died. The text says, “Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus” (John 11:5). They were Jesus’ friends in Bethany; theirs was the home where he often ate and rested. Now Mary fell at his feet, weeping: “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died” (John 11:32).

There was hurt in those words, and a bit of blame. Jesus didn’t defend himself, and he didn’t immediately deliver a lesson on the resurrection. The text says “he groaned in the spirit and was troubled” (John 11:33), and then comes the shortest verse in the whole Bible: “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). Those watching said, “See how much affection he had for him!” (John 11:36). He knew full well that within minutes he would raise Lazarus from the dead, yet he first wept with his friends.

This is Jesus’ lesson in friendship: when a friend is hurting most, first be present, then speak. Our common mistake is rushing to give answers: “It’s all God’s good plan.” “Be strong!” “At least he’s gone to heaven.” These may all be true, but said too soon, they rub salt into the wound. Job’s friends were at their best during those first seven days, when “they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him” (Job 2:13). Later, when they started explaining things, they only added to his burden.

Today’s practice is simple. Think of someone going through a loss—a death in the family, a breakup, a job loss, an illness, homesickness after moving abroad. Go be with them, or send them a message. It doesn’t need to be long, and you don’t need to explain God’s will. Just say, “I know you’re hurting, and I’m here. Can I take you out for a meal, or just come sit with you for a while?” Then actually go. Sometimes the most spiritual words are the tears we shed together.
lessons.light: “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). This is selfless love: setting aside the wisdom I want to show off and entering into someone else’s pain. Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head—those who rely on their heads rush to explain; those who lead with the heart know how to stay present. Jesus’ tears let Mary know she wasn’t alone.
think: Before raising Lazarus, what did Jesus do first?
When friends are suffering, am I too quick to give answers or explanations?
Whom will I keep company with today who is going through a loss, and how?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you wept at your friend’s tomb, and your tears tell me you understand our pain. Take away my urge to rush in with answers, and teach me to keep quiet company and weep with those who weep. Lead me today to someone who is grieving, so that through my presence they may sense yours. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact someone who is going through a loss. Don’t explain anything—just say, “I’m here,” and set a specific time to visit or share a meal with them.
lessons.quick: When a friend is hurting most, weep with them first, then speak.
text: When she had said this, she went away and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here and is calling you.”
When she heard this, she arose quickly and went to him.
Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him.
Then the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.”
Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.”
When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit and was troubled,
and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.”
Jesus wept.
The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!”
Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?”

lessons.title: Couldn’t You Watch with Me One Hour?
lessons.hear:
Gethsemane was the night in Jesus’ life when he most needed his friends. He took Peter, James, and John further in with him and openly shared the pain in his heart: “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). The Lord of the universe was telling his friends: I need you.

And what happened? He came back from praying and found them asleep. “What, couldn’t you watch with me for one hour?” (Matthew 26:40). Once, twice, three times. It wasn’t that the disciples didn’t love Jesus. Jesus himself said, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41). They were simply tired, and they didn’t understand how important that night was.

Today, use this scene to examine yourself. Do I often “fall asleep” when my friends need me? Not deliberately ignoring them, just too busy, too tired, too focused on my own stuff. A friend posts in the group chat, “I’m so exhausted lately,” and I tap a sticker and scroll on. A friend is in the hospital, and I say, “I’ll come see you when I have time,” but I never have time. A friend says they’d like to talk, and I say, “Another day,” and that day never comes. Self-centered friendship only shows up when it’s convenient.

But at the end of this passage, Jesus didn’t say, “You’re not worthy to be my friends.” He said, “Arise, let’s be going” (Matthew 26:46). He still counted them as his companions. He even addressed Judas, who had come to betray him, as “Friend” (Matthew 26:50). In Jesus, our failed friendships still have a chance to be restored. So today’s adjustment is very concrete: think of a friend you missed because you were “asleep,” send them a message admitting your neglect, and offer the care that is overdue.
lessons.light: Self-centered friendship shows up only when it’s convenient; selfless friendship stays awake when the other person is in need. We review not to beat ourselves up but to adjust. After the disciples slept, Jesus still said, “Let’s be going.” His grace lets us start over and become a friend who stays awake.
think: What did Jesus ask of his disciples in Gethsemane, and how did they respond?
Which friend recently needed me while I was “asleep”?
How will I offer that friend my overdue care today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on your most painful night you needed your friends, but the disciples fell asleep—and I often do the same. Forgive me for showing up only when it’s convenient and missing my friends’ needs. Thank you that you still say, “Arise, let’s be going.” Keep me awake, so that I stay by my friends’ side when they need me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a friend whose need you once missed. Simply say, “I’m sorry I wasn’t there for you last time,” and ask how they’re doing now and what they need.
lessons.quick: Staying awake when a friend needs me is more like Jesus than showing up when it’s convenient.
text: Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.”
He took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and severely troubled.
Then Jesus said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me.”
He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.”
He came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “What, couldn’t you watch with me for one hour?
Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying, “My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done.”
He came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
He left them again, went away, and prayed a third time, saying the same words.
Then he came to his disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.
Arise, let’s be going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.”

lessons.title: “Come and See” Friendship
lessons.hear:
How did Jesus’ first disciples come to him? Not through a big evangelistic rally, but through friendship. After Andrew met Jesus, “He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, ‘We have found the Messiah!’” (John 1:41). Then “He brought him to Jesus” (John 1:42). The next day, Philip also went to find his friend Nathanael.

Nathanael’s response was blunt, even a little sarcastic: “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). Philip didn’t argue with him or get upset. He said just three words: “Come and see.” This is gospel friendship at its most beautiful: no pressure, no debate—just inviting a friend to come and meet for themselves the Friend who changed my life.

This week we have learned from Jesus how to be a friend. He calls us friends and opens his heart to us. He befriends the excluded. He weeps with those who weep. He still invites us to get up when we fail. When we have been loved by a friendship like that, we naturally want to introduce this Friend to our friends. The gospel is not a sales quota, and friends are not targets; friendship has value in itself, and the gospel is the natural overflow of love.

Today, go over what you received this week again, and pass it on. In the app’s Five Names list, you can write down five friends you care about who don’t yet know Jesus, and pray for them every day. Or take an even simpler first step: choose a brother or sister you trust, tell them what “Jesus calls me friend” has meant to you this week, and invite them to pray with you for those five names. One day, when your friend asks about your faith, you too can say gently, like Philip, “Come and see.”
lessons.light: Multiplication isn’t salesmanship; it is letting friendship become a channel through which grace flows. The “2” in 235 means becoming spiritual companions with selfless people; when two people pray together for their friends, gospel friendship has begun. Let Jesus receive all the glory: we are not introducing ourselves, but the best Friend of all.
think: How did Andrew and Philip bring their friends to Jesus?
Have I turned gospel friendship into pressure or a quota?
Who are my Five Names, and whom will I invite today to pray for them with me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling me your friend, and thank you for using friends to bring me to you. Make my friendships sincere and free of hidden agendas, and let your love overflow naturally through me. I place my five friends in your hands. At the right time, let me be able to say gently, “Come and see.” In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down in the app’s Five Names five friends you care about who don’t yet believe in Jesus. Then invite a brother or sister to pray for them with you this week.
lessons.quick: Like Philip—no arguing, no pressure, just “Come and see.”
text: One of the two who heard John and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).
On the next day, he was determined to go out into Galilee, and he found Philip. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.”
Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the law and also the prophets, wrote: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”

weeks.title: David and Jonathan: Covenant Friendship
weeks.theme: True friendship is a covenant, not a transaction; Jonathan took off his robe and selflessly helped David fulfill his calling.
group: Read 1 Samuel 18:1-4 and 23:16-18. What did Jonathan lay down for David?
When a friend outshines you, is your heart more like Jonathan’s or more like Saul’s?
How will you help a friend flourish this week, and what is one concrete way you will love your neighbor?
weeks.sunday: Invite a longtime friend (or their family) over for a meal, or meet somewhere convenient for them. Before you go, pray for them and ask the Lord to help you see the gifts in their life. When you meet, tell them specifically what you appreciate about them, and ask what they would like you to pray about with them. When you get home, give thanks for the covenant of this friendship and write down their prayer requests.

lessons.title: Souls Knit Together
lessons.hear:
David had just killed Goliath and was standing before King Saul, speaking with him. At that very moment, the text says, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:1). Then, “Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:3).

This was a highly unusual friendship. Jonathan was a prince, heir to the throne; David was a young shepherd fresh from the fields. By ordinary logic, David was the person Jonathan should have guarded against most. But Jonathan did something astonishing: he “stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David with his clothing, even including his sword, his bow, and his sash” (1 Samuel 18:4). The robe and weapons were signs of a prince’s identity and power. In effect, he was saying, “Everything I have, I am willing to share with you. You fit God’s purpose better than I do.”

Here we see the difference between covenant friendship and transactional friendship. Transactional friendship is like doing business: I’m good to you only if you’re good to me; I keep you around as long as you’re useful; once I come out on the losing end, we part ways. Covenant friendship is like the vows of marriage: it isn’t built on the other person’s performance but on a promise, with God as witness. Jonathan later reminded David that they had sworn in the LORD’s name, saying, “The LORD is between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever” (1 Samuel 20:42). When God stands between two friends, the friendship is no longer just two people’s feelings; it has an eternal foundation.

This week we will learn this kind of friendship. You may be thinking, “I don’t have a Jonathan in my life.” But God’s invitation is this: first become someone else’s Jonathan. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you whom God has placed beside you to love with a covenant heart.
lessons.light: Jonathan models selfless friendship—not having no self, but not making himself the center. Taking off his robe was like letting God reign and letting God’s chosen one take first place. Transactional friendship asks, “What do I get?” Covenant friendship asks, “How does God want me to help this person flourish?” Jesus is my example: what he made with us is a covenant that will never be broken.
think: What did the robe and weapons Jonathan gave David signify?
Are my friendships more like covenants or more like transactions?
What “robe” can I share with a friend today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you made a new covenant with me and gave yourself for me through your precious blood; you are my truest covenant friend. Remove transactional friendship from my heart. Make me like Jonathan, willing to take off my robe, share all I have, and love those you have placed beside me with a covenant heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a friend and share one specific resource you have—time, a skill, connections, or something you own—such as helping them revise a résumé or going with them to run an errand.
lessons.quick: Transactional friendship asks if you’re useful; covenant friendship asks what God intends.
text: When he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Saul took him that day, and wouldn’t let him go home to his father’s house any more.
Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David with his clothing, even including his sword, his bow, and his sash.
David went out wherever Saul sent him, and behaved himself wisely; and Saul set him over the men of war. It was good in the sight of all the people, and also in the sight of Saul’s servants.

lessons.title: You Will Be King, I Will Be Next to You
lessons.hear:
Two sisters had known each other through their fellowship for over ten years. They prayed together and led worship together. Then the church invited one of them to become a small group leader, and the other wasn’t chosen. Outwardly, the one who wasn’t chosen smiled and offered congratulations. But from that day on, she rarely replied to her friend’s messages, and whenever her friend shared in small group, she kept her eyes on her phone. A voice in her heart kept asking, “Why her and not me?”

This is an old mindset very familiar in Chinese culture: even friends must compare. At class reunions we compare salaries, houses, and our children’s grades; in group chats we compare vacation photos. We say, “I’m so happy for you,” while keeping score inside. In this mindset, my friend’s success is my failure.

Now look at Jonathan. David was being hunted by Saul and hiding in the woods of the wilderness of Ziph. Then “Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). He didn’t go to pour out his own troubles; he went to strengthen his friend’s faith. Then he said something astonishing: “You will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you” (1 Samuel 23:17). The one who should have been king willingly stepped into second place, because he saw God’s purpose.

This is God’s perspective: in God’s kingdom, a friend’s success is not my failure but a display of God’s grace. When I fix my focus on Jesus, I no longer need to measure myself against my friends; instead, I can truly rejoice with them. Later, as that sister read this passage in prayer, she wept for a long time. She reached out and invited her friend for coffee, honestly confessed her jealousy, and said, “I want to be your right hand and help you lead this small group well.” That day their friendship didn’t break apart; it grew deeper.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Jonathan laid down power and returned to his proper place—he not only helped David fulfill his calling but also became the most beautiful version of himself. Our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves and not on the spotlight others are standing in. When our perspective changes, we move from comparing to championing.
think: When Jonathan went to see David, what two things did he do?
Whose recent success has made me uncomfortable inside?
How can I concretely “strengthen the hand” of that friend instead of comparing myself with them?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often compare myself with my friends—congratulating them with my lips while keeping score in my heart. Forgive my jealousy. Make me like Jonathan, seeing your purpose and gladly standing next to my friend in second place. Help me today to rejoice sincerely in my friend’s success and to strengthen them with your word. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a friend who has had good news recently. Tell them specifically what you thank God for in their life, and send them a Bible verse as a blessing.
lessons.quick: My friend is king, and I gladly stand next to them—that is selfless friendship.
text: David stayed in the wilderness in the strongholds, and remained in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul sought him every day, but God didn’t deliver him into his hand.
David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph in the woods.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God.
He said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for the hand of Saul my father won’t find you; and you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you; and Saul my father knows that also.”
They both made a covenant before the LORD. Then David stayed in the woods and Jonathan went to his house.

lessons.title: Speaking Up for an Absent Friend
lessons.hear:
Saul openly told all his servants that he wanted David killed. It was the kind of setting where everyone chooses silence, because whoever speaks up for David offends the king. But the text says, “Jonathan spoke good of David to Saul his father” (1 Samuel 19:4).

Notice what Jonathan said. He didn’t plead vaguely; he stated specific facts: “he has not sinned against you, and because his works have been very good toward you” (1 Samuel 19:4). He reminded his father that David had put his life in his hand to strike down the Philistine, and that through him the LORD had worked a great victory. Jonathan risked his father’s fury to stand up for a friend who wasn’t in the room. As a result, Saul changed his mind for a time and swore he would not kill David.

This is a very concrete—and rarely discussed—practice of covenant friendship: protecting your friend’s reputation when they aren’t there. Today, “killing David” rarely involves real swords. More often it’s a snide remark in a group chat, a round of laughter over dinner, a whisper by the office coffee machine: “Oh, him? You know what he’s like…” In those moments, most people stay silent, not wanting to offend the speaker and afraid of getting dragged in themselves.

Today’s practice is to be a friend who “speaks good of David.” When someone talks about your friend behind their back, you can say gently but clearly, “That’s not the person I know—he helped me a lot just recently.” Or, “It might be better to ask him directly about that.” You don’t have to pick a fight; you just refuse to let lies or gossip pass unchallenged in front of you. If no such moment comes up today, you can take the initiative: publicly affirm a friend’s hard work in a group chat or gathering. Speaking good words out loud is like guarding the door for your friend while they’re away.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than saving face. Speaking up for a friend costs something—that is self-denial: for Jesus, for others, not for myself. The “0” in 920 stands for selflessness—not afraid of being dragged in, caring only about my friend’s good name and God’s justice. Word Watch is not only about not speaking ill; it also means bravely speaking good.
think: When Jonathan spoke up for David, what specific facts did he state?
When someone talks about my friend behind their back, how do I usually respond?
Where today can I publicly affirm a friend?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you intercede for me before the Father and speak on my behalf. Give me Jonathan’s courage to protect my friends’ reputations when they aren’t there, and not to let gossip pass unchallenged in front of me. Let my mouth speak words that build others up and benefit those who hear. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in a group chat or gathering, specifically affirm a friend’s recent hard work. If you hear someone talking about a friend, gently put in a fair word for them.
lessons.quick: When a friend isn’t in the room, guard the door for them.
text: Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul’s son, greatly delighted in David.
Jonathan told David, saying, “Saul my father seeks to kill you. Now therefore, please take care of yourself in the morning, live in a secret place, and hide yourself.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will talk with my father about you; and if I see anything, I will tell you.”

Jonathan spoke good of David to Saul his father, and said to him, “Don’t let the king sin against his servant, against David; because he has not sinned against you, and because his works have been very good toward you;

for he put his life in his hand and struck the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great victory for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood, to kill David without a cause?”
Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan; and Saul swore, “As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death.”
Jonathan called David, and Jonathan showed him all those things. Then Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.

lessons.title: Watched from That Day On
lessons.hear:
The same victory produced completely different fruit in two hearts. When Jonathan saw David triumph, he loved him as his own soul. But when Saul heard the women singing, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7), he was furious. He said, “They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?” (1 Samuel 18:8).

Then the text records a heavy sentence: “Saul watched David from that day and forward” (1 Samuel 18:9). One song, one comparison, lit a lifetime of jealousy. Saul went on to hunt David for years, draining his kingdom’s strength and destroying his own family. What makes jealousy so dangerous is that it causes us to see God’s blessing as a threat, and to see comrades who should stand with us as enemies.

Today, use this passage to examine yourself honestly. When a friend posts about a promotion, a new house, an overseas trip, or a child getting into a good school, what is my first reaction? Do I rejoice for them, or do I quietly start counting “thousands” and “ten thousands”? When someone at church is more popular or more valued than I am, do I begin to eye them suspiciously—picking at their faults in my heart, dropping a light put-down in front of others? These are all marks of the self-centered life: I have put myself at the center, so other people’s shine hurts my eyes.

The way to adjust is the path Jonathan walked. First, admit the jealousy; don’t hide it, but bring it to God. Second, let Jesus reign—acknowledge that God is the one who assigns gifts and positions, not me. Third, do something that runs opposite to jealousy: pray a blessing over that friend and look for a chance to praise them sincerely. In prayer and blessing, jealousy slowly loses its power.
lessons.light: Jealousy is another face of pride: leaving our proper place and wanting to sit where glory is handed out. Letting Jesus reign means acknowledging that the thousands and the ten thousands are both God’s to assign. From the same victory, the self-centered see a threat; the selfless see God’s grace. After review comes adjustment: replacing comparison with blessing.
think: From the same victory, how did Jonathan’s and Saul’s reactions differ?
Whose recent news has me quietly counting “thousands” and “ten thousands”?
Whom will I bless in prayer and sincerely praise today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that Saul’s suspicious eye is in my heart too; when my friends are blessed, I often compare before I bless. Forgive my jealousy. Reign in my heart, and help me acknowledge that every gift and position is yours to assign. Make me like Jonathan, able to rejoice sincerely with my friends. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a friend you feel a little jealous of. Spend three minutes praying specific blessings over them, then send them a message sincerely praising one thing about them.
lessons.quick: Jealousy turns friends into enemies; blessing turns rivals back into comrades.
text: As they came, when David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul with tambourines, with joy, and with instruments of music.
The women sang to one another as they played, and said, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, “They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?”
Saul watched David from that day and forward.
On the next day, an evil spirit from God came mightily on Saul, and he prophesied in the middle of the house. David played with his hand, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand;
and Saul threw the spear, for he said, “I will pin David to the wall!” David escaped from his presence twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him, and had departed from Saul.

lessons.title: For Jonathan’s Sake
lessons.hear:
Many years after Jonathan died in battle, David had become king and his throne was secure. One day he asked, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” (2 Samuel 9:1). In the ancient world, a new king often wiped out the descendants of the previous dynasty. But David remembered his covenant with Jonathan—a covenant not only between the two of them, but “between my offspring and your offspring, forever” (1 Samuel 20:42).

They found Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, who was lame. When Mephibosheth came before David, he fell on his face, his heart probably full of fear. But David said, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake … You will eat bread at my table continually” (2 Samuel 9:7). A friendship was still blessing the next generation many years after one friend had died. This is the power of covenant friendship: it doesn’t change with circumstances, and it doesn’t end with death.

David had once lamented for Jonathan: “I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan. You have been very pleasant to me” (2 Samuel 1:26). Yet his most beautiful memorial was not a song of mourning, but a table prepared for his friend’s son. This reminds us of the gospel: like Mephibosheth, we are lame and unworthy, yet for Christ’s sake God lets us eat at his table continually.

This week we have seen that true friendship is a covenant, not a transaction; that when my friend is king, I gladly stand next to him; that we speak up for friends who aren’t in the room; and that when jealousy rises, we choose to bless. Today, pass this friendship on. Maybe that means caring for a friend’s parents or children. Maybe it means telling your children, students, or small group members, “I have a friend like this, and he taught me what faithfulness is.” Let the next generation see that in Christ there is a kind of friendship that goes on and on.
lessons.light: Multiplication means letting the covenant blessing reach the next generation. The “3” in 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children: David showing kindness to Mephibosheth for Jonathan’s sake is friendship extended into a spiritual family. Let Jesus receive all the glory, because we too have been invited to the King’s table for his sake.
think: Why did David look for someone left from Saul’s house, and how did he treat Mephibosheth?
Do my friendships shift with circumstances, or do they carry covenant commitment?
How will I bless a friend’s family today, or pass the story of this friendship on to the next generation?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, like Mephibosheth I am unworthy, yet for Christ’s sake you invite me to eat at your table continually. Thank you for your covenant-keeping love. Give my friendships covenant commitment that doesn’t shift with circumstances, and help me pass this faithfulness on to the next generation so they can see your faithfulness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, show care for a friend’s family member—a parent, child, or spouse—by sending a greeting or a small gift. At dinner, share with your family about a friendship that has shaped you.
lessons.quick: The covenant of true friendship reaches all the way to the next generation’s table.
text: David said, “Is there yet any who is left of Saul’s house, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was of Saul’s house a servant whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David; and the king said to him, “Are you Ziba?” He said, “I am your servant.”
The king said, “Is there not yet any of Saul’s house, that I may show the kindness of God to him?” Ziba said to the king, “Jonathan still has a son, who is lame in his feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar.”
Then King David sent and brought him out of the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo Debar.
Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, fell on his face, and showed respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Behold, your servant!”

David said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and will restore to you all the land of Saul your father. You will eat bread at my table continually.”

weeks.keyText: Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.

weeks.title: Iron Sharpens Iron: Friendships That Grow Us
weeks.theme: Good friends don’t just laugh with you; they speak the truth in love and sharpen one another into the likeness of Christ.
group: Read Proverbs 27:5-10. How does Solomon describe the difference between true friends and false friends?
Is it harder for you to speak honestly to a friend, or to accept a friend’s correction? Why?
How will you spur a friend on to good works this week, and what is one concrete way you will love your neighbor?
weeks.sunday: Arrange to have breakfast or take a walk this weekend with one or two trusted brothers or sisters (ideally of the same gender). Before you meet, each of you pray that the Lord will help you speak the truth in love. When you’re together, take turns sharing: “One thing I most need to be reminded of lately.” Pray for one another, and agree to check in on each other’s progress with a message next week. When you get home, thank God for the friends he has given to sharpen you.

lessons.title: The Wounds of a Friend
lessons.hear:
In Proverbs, Solomon included a saying that isn’t very pleasant to hear but is truly precious: “Better is open rebuke than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5). Then he adds: “The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse” (Proverbs 27:6).

These two sayings turn our idea of friendship upside down. We assume a good friend is someone who makes us comfortable—always supportive, always liking our posts, always saying “You’re not wrong.” But Proverbs says a true friend will sometimes cause you pain, because they are willing to risk the relationship cooling in order to tell you the truth. Meanwhile, those who only offer profuse kisses may seem warm on the surface, but they never take responsibility for your life.

Solomon also says, “Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart; so does earnest counsel from a man’s friend” (Proverbs 27:9). Honest counsel may grate on the ear at first, but later it lingers in the heart like a fragrance. That is why this week’s memory verse is: “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance” (Proverbs 27:17).

Picture two knives. If they simply sit side by side without touching, they will never get sharper. To sharpen a blade, there will be friction and sparks. But the friction isn’t meant to ruin the other blade; it’s meant to make it more useful. Christian friendship works the same way. God places friends beside us not only to pass the time with us, but so that we can grind away each other’s self-centered rust and sharpen one another into the likeness of Christ.

So today, begin by thanking God for the friends in your life who have told you the truth. Maybe you weren’t comfortable at the time, or you even got angry. But looking back, those were the very moments when God was using them to sharpen you.
lessons.light: Self-centered friendship wants only comfort and fears friction; selfless friendship is willing to pay the price of being disliked for the other person’s growth. Among the eight steps of changing a mindset are review and adjustment—and God often uses a friend’s words to help us see blind spots we can’t see ourselves.
think: How do Proverbs 27:5-6 and 27:9 describe a “faithful friend”?
Do I have a friend who tells me the truth? How do I respond to them?
How can I thank someone today who once told me the truth?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for placing friends in my life who tell me the truth. I confess that I often prefer to hear pleasant words and avoid honest counsel. Help me treasure the faithful wounds of a friend, and make me a friend who sharpens others in love, so that together we become more like Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, message a friend who once told you the truth and helped you grow. Thank them specifically for that reminder, and tell them how their words helped you.
lessons.quick: The wounds of a friend are faithful—iron sharpening iron.
text: Better is open rebuke than hidden love.
The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.
A full soul loathes a honeycomb; but to a hungry soul, every bitter thing is sweet.
As a bird that wanders from her nest, so is a man who wanders from his home.
Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart; so does earnest counsel from a man’s friend.
Don’t forsake your friend and your father’s friend. Don’t go to your brother’s house in the day of your disaster. A neighbor who is near is better than a distant brother.

lessons.title: A Servant’s Honest Word
lessons.hear:
A young sister was helping a senior ministry leader at church plan an event. She noticed that whenever this older woman heard a different opinion in a meeting, her face darkened and she said, “I was serving before you were even born.” After that, several new team members stopped speaking up. The sister wanted to say something, but she thought, “I’m just a younger person—who am I to say anything?”

This is a deep-rooted old mindset in Chinese culture: speaking the truth flows from elders to juniors, and those in higher positions don’t need to listen. Yet the Bible tells of a very important man who was sharpened by a few “little people.” Naaman, commander of the army of Aram, had leprosy. He came to Elisha’s door, but the prophet only sent a messenger telling him to go wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman was furious: “Behold, I thought, ‘He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place, and heal the leper’” (2 Kings 5:11). He had already written the script for his own healing, and when the script was disrupted, he turned and walked away.

Then his servants came near and said, “My father, if the prophet had asked you do some great thing, wouldn’t you have done it? How much rather then, when he says to you, ‘Wash, and be clean’?” (2 Kings 5:13). Look at how they spoke the truth: they began by calling him “My father,” with respect; they used a question instead of an accusation; and they focused on his good rather than on proving they knew better. That is iron sharpening iron: the blade is aimed at the rust, not at the person.

Naaman also did something very hard for an important man: he listened. “Then went he down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child” (2 Kings 5:14). God’s perspective convinces us: “One who rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than one who flatters with the tongue” (Proverbs 28:23). Truth-telling isn’t about seniority; it’s about love.

After praying, that sister found a private moment and said, “I really respect your experience. The new team members actually want to learn from you—they’re just a bit afraid to speak up in meetings.” The older woman was silent for a long time. At the next meeting, the first thing she said was, “If anyone has a different idea, please share it.”
lessons.light: Pride needs a grand show, just as Naaman wanted the prophet to come out to him; humility can hear God’s voice from the mouth of a servant. Selfless people don’t look at the speaker’s rank; they only ask whether the words come from God. Those who speak the truth must also be selfless—respectful, gentle, seeking the other’s good—letting Jesus reign, not letting “I’m right” reign.
think: In 2 Kings 5:11-14, how did the servants counsel Naaman, and how did he respond?
Because of seniority or position, have I been afraid to speak—or unwilling to hear—an honest word?
How can I speak the truth to a friend with respect and a question?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that sometimes I am like Naaman, wanting to be treated according to my own script. At other times I am afraid of rank or of offending people, so I don’t dare speak the truth. Give me humble ears to hear your reminders from anyone’s mouth, and give me gentle courage to speak the truth for my friend’s good. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone you have long wanted to say something to but haven’t, because of seniority or saving face. Pray for them first, then write out a sentence that begins with respect and uses a question instead of an accusation, and find a private moment to say it.
lessons.quick: Truth-telling isn’t about seniority but love—and those who listen are made clean.
text: So Naaman came with his horses and with his chariots, and stood at the door of the house of Elisha.
Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, “Go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh shall come again to you, and you shall be clean.”

But Naaman was angry, and went away and said, “Behold, I thought, ‘He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the place, and heal the leper.’
Aren’t Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn’t I wash in them and be clean?” So he turned and went away in a rage.

His servants came near and spoke to him, and said, “My father, if the prophet had asked you do some great thing, wouldn’t you have done it? How much rather then, when he says to you, ‘Wash, and be clean’?”
Then went he down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

lessons.title: Provoking One Another to Love
lessons.hear:
“Iron sharpens iron” isn’t only about correction; it also includes encouragement. Hebrews says, “Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24).

“Provoke” is a strong word. Here it means to stir up or spark—like gently blowing on a bed of coals so that a fire about to go out flares up again. A true friend doesn’t only help you up when you fall; they rekindle you when you’re discouraged. They don’t only point out where you’re wrong; they also remind you of the good things God has placed in you.

This passage holds two more important reminders. First, “consider”: to pay attention, to take notice. To encourage someone, you must first see them. Many people do want to encourage their friends, but they are too busy to notice what those friends have been doing or struggling with lately. Second, “not forsaking our own assembling together” (Hebrews 10:25). Sharpening requires contact; friendship needs face-to-face time. Stickers in a group chat are convenient, but they can’t replace eating together, praying together, and serving together.

Today’s practice: be the breath that blows on someone’s coals. First, think of a friend and pay attention to how they have been doing. Maybe they just started serving at church but feel timid. Maybe they are caring for aging parents and are worn out. Maybe they are working hard to break a bad habit. Then encourage them specifically. Don’t just say, “You’ve got this!” Tell them what you have seen: “I’ve noticed you’ve been visiting your mom every week lately. That’s not easy, and God surely remembers it.” One specific word of encouragement kindles a heart more than ten vague compliments. If possible, invite them to join you at a gathering this week, or to serve alongside you.
lessons.light: The “9” in 920 is the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit; provoking one another to love helps the fruit in our friends’ lives grow better. Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart: the Spirit lets us see God at work in our friends and gives us a timely word, like a breath on the coals. Jesus is my example: when his disciples were discouraged, he often pointed out the Father’s purpose for them.
think: What concrete ways of building one another up are mentioned in Hebrews 10:24-25?
Have I been so busy lately that I haven’t paid attention to how my friends are doing?
Which friend will I specifically encourage today, and what have I seen in them that I will name?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, open my eyes to notice the struggles and efforts of the friends around me. Let me do more than say, “You’ve got this”—let me name what you are doing in their lives. Today, make my words like a breath on their coals, kindling their love, so that we grow together in the Lord. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a friend and send a specific message of encouragement naming one thing you’ve seen them do well. Invite them to join you at a gathering or in serving this week.
lessons.quick: Specific encouragement is a breath blown on a friend’s coals.
text: let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful.
Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.

lessons.title: Blessed Is Your Discretion
lessons.hear:
After Nabal insulted him, David set out in a rage with four hundred men to take revenge. When Nabal’s wife Abigail heard, she hurried out to meet him with gifts, bowed down before David, and courageously urged him not to avenge himself or shed innocent blood, so that later this would be no “offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself” (1 Samuel 25:31).

A man in the heat of anger, sword in hand, is the hardest person to talk sense into. But David stopped, and he even said: “Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand” (1 Samuel 25:33). Far from lashing out in wounded pride, he thanked the one who had stopped him: “I have listened to your voice and have granted your request” (1 Samuel 25:35). This is what it looks like to receive correction humbly.

Today, review yourself from two angles. First, how do I receive correction? David later wrote: “Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head” (Psalm 141:5). The self-centered, once corrected, defend themselves, dig up old grievances, give the silent treatment, or even block the other person. The selfless can say, “Thank you. I’ll think that over carefully.”

Second, how do I give correction? Abigail humbly bowed down first, then spoke the truth. Paul also reminds us: “you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself” (Galatians 6:1). If all I do is complain behind someone’s back, or humiliate them publicly with sarcasm, that isn’t iron sharpening iron; it’s iron smashing iron. Even the apostles corrected one another face to face: Paul once confronted Peter at Antioch about his inconsistency (see Galatians 2:11-14), yet Peter later still called him “our beloved brother Paul” (2 Peter 3:15). Sincere, gentle friction can produce a deeper friendship. Today, consider: who has recently reminded you of something, and you still haven’t responded well?
lessons.light: Rushing to defend ourselves when corrected is the self-centered life protecting itself; receiving correction humbly is returning to our proper place, admitting that I too need sharpening. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. The stories of David and Abigail, and of Peter and Paul, show that sincere friction can produce deeper friendships.
think: How did Abigail dissuade David, and how did David respond to her?
The last time I was corrected, did I defend myself, go silent, or humbly accept it?
To whom who has corrected me will I say, “Thank you—you were right”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that when I’m corrected I often rush to defend myself, and I even lash out in wounded pride. Give me a heart that humbly receives correction and counts a friend’s rebuke as oil on my head. Give me gentleness and courage as well, so that when needed I restore my friends in love instead of talking about them behind their backs. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone who recently corrected you, and take the initiative to say, “Thank you for what you told me. I’ve thought it over, and you were right.” Share how you plan to change.
lessons.quick: Iron that refuses to be sharpened will never gain an edge.
text: David said to Abigail, “Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me!
Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.

For indeed, as the LORD the God of Israel lives, who has withheld me from harming you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, surely there wouldn’t have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
So David received from her hand that which she had brought him. Then he said to her, “Go up in peace to your house. Behold, I have listened to your voice and have granted your request.”

lessons.title: While It Is Called “Today”
lessons.hear:
The writer of Hebrews says: “exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today’, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). Notice two phrases: “today” and “day by day.” A hardened heart rarely happens overnight. Like mineral buildup in a water pipe, it accumulates bit by bit. So exhorting one another can’t wait until something major goes wrong; it needs to become a daily habit. Paul likewise urged believers: “Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do” (1 Thessalonians 5:11).

Good companions learn to discern what a friend needs right now: sometimes a reminder, sometimes a boost, sometimes practical help—and everyone needs patience. Iron-sharpens-iron friendship isn’t only about grinding; it knows how to say the right word at the right time.

This week we have seen that the wounds of a friend are faithful; that true friends, like Naaman’s servants, are willing to speak the truth; that they are like a breath on the coals, provoking one another to love; and that we learn to correct gently and to receive correction humbly. Now let’s turn this kind of friendship into a habit.

Here is a concrete way to do it: find one or two brothers or sisters of the same gender and form a “sharpening group.” You might meet every two weeks, or talk by phone once a week, and ask each other three simple questions: “How is your relationship with God lately?” “Is there anything you need me to remind you of?” “How can I pray for you?” This is what the 321 Vision calls spiritual companions. One knife can’t sharpen itself; it takes two. A solitary spiritual life rusts easily, but with companions we can grow together. Today, invite a friend to begin this journey with you, and share with them what you received this week.
lessons.light: The “2” in 235 means becoming spiritual companions with selfless people. Iron-sharpens-iron friendship can’t rely on a moment of inspiration; it relies on repetition—doing it as a matter of course until it becomes a habit. As such companionships multiply in the church, we are building God’s system, and the Lord’s Prayer is fulfilled in one small circle after another.
think: Why does Hebrews 3:13 emphasize exhorting one another “today” and “day by day”?
Do I have a spiritual companion with whom I can sharpen and be sharpened?
Whom will I invite this week to start a group that meets regularly to build one another up?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that you don’t make me walk the spiritual road alone. Provide companions with whom I can sharpen and be sharpened, and make me a trustworthy companion for others. Help us exhort and build one another up as a matter of course, knowing when to remind, when to encourage, and when to support, so that together we grow into the likeness of Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, invite a brother or sister of the same gender to agree to meet or talk every two weeks for the next month, asking each other those three questions and praying for one another.
lessons.quick: One knife can’t sharpen itself—find a companion and sharpen together.
text: Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there might be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God;
but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called “today”, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end,

weeks.keyText: Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.

weeks.title: Choosing Friends, Becoming a Friend
weeks.theme: Whoever you walk with determines where you end up—so walk with the wise, and resolve to be a good friend to others.
group: Read Psalm 1:1-3. How does the progression of “walk, stand, sit” play out in our social lives today?
Which friend has drawn you closer to God, and what did they do?
Whose good friend will you become this week, and what is one concrete way you will love your neighbor?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, invite a younger brother or sister, or someone new to your church, to a meal at your home or a nearby restaurant. Before you go, pray for them and ask the Lord to make you a good companion to them. Over the meal, listen as they talk about their circle of friends and their life, and share a time when a friend brought you closer to God. When you get home, give thanks for them and keep praying for them.

lessons.title: A Tree Planted by the Streams
lessons.hear:
Psalm 1 is like the front door to the whole book of Psalms. It opens by talking about the direction of a life: “Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers” (Psalm 1:1). Notice the three verbs: walk, stand, sit. At first you simply go along with their advice; then you stop and linger on their path; finally you sit right down and become part of the circle. The direction of a life is often carried off just like that, step by step, by the people around us.

Solomon puts it even more directly: “One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm” (Proverbs 13:20). Friends are like air—we breathe them in every day without much notice, but over time our bodies know whether we have been breathing fresh air or smoke. The group chats you’re most active in, the coworkers you usually eat with, the person you text late at night—all of them are quietly shaping how you talk, how you spend money, how you see people, even how warm your heart is toward God.

What does the blessed person look like? “His delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2). His roots go down first into God’s word, so “He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither” (Psalm 1:3). Notice that this tree isn’t planted in a greenhouse sealed off from the world. It grows right out in the fields of ordinary life—its roots are simply by the streams.

This also helps us discern. Jesus is the friend of sinners, and we too are to love people who don’t yet know God; but our roots must not grow into their values. The key question is who is influencing whom: Am I bringing the life of Christ into that circle, or is that circle carrying me away from Christ? This week we will learn two things: to choose carefully the friends who shape us, and to resolve to become a friend who brings others closer to God.
lessons.light: Change your perspective and your mindset will change. From a human perspective, friends are for fun and networking; from God’s perspective, friends shape the direction of my life. The order of relationships is God first, then people: when my roots go down first into God’s word, I can stand firm among people and become someone who brings life.
think: What gradual progression does “walk, stand, sit” in Psalm 1:1 describe?
Who are the three people or groups that most influence how I talk and think?
How will I let my roots grow deeper into God’s word this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for promising that I can be like a tree planted by the streams of water. I confess that I am often carried away by the voices around me without realizing it. Let my roots go down first into your word. Help me choose carefully the friends who shape me, and make me someone who brings life to my circle of friends rather than someone who is carried away from you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the five people or groups you interact with most, and honestly mark each one: Does this draw me closer to God or further away? Then pray for each of them.
lessons.quick: Whoever you walk with determines where you go.
text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
but his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
The wicked are not so, but are like the chaff which the wind drives away.
Therefore the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.
For the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.

lessons.title: Rehoboam’s Inner Circle
lessons.hear:
A young brother fresh out of school joined a company with a very “lively” culture. The coworkers who started with him quickly became good friends; after work they would grab late-night food and play video games together. Gradually he noticed that they often taught one another how to pad expense reports and how to put on a show for the boss, and their jokes about people grew more and more cutting. He thought, “I have a mind of my own. I’m just listening; it won’t affect me.” Six months later, he found some “everybody does it” numbers creeping onto his own expense reports.

This is a common old mindset: friends are just people to hang out with; they won’t change me. But the Bible says, “Don’t be deceived! ‘Evil companionships corrupt good morals’” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Look at Solomon’s son Rehoboam. He had just taken the throne, and the people asked him to lighten their heavy burden. He first consulted the old men, who said: “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever” (1 Kings 12:7). That was mature and godly advice. But “he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him” (1 Kings 12:8). These companions told him to be even harsher, even putting these words in his mouth: “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist” (1 Kings 12:10). Rehoboam did as they said, and from then on the kingdom was divided.

It wasn’t that Rehoboam never heard good advice; he chose to listen to friends who made him comfortable and were just like him. This is God’s perspective: friends don’t just keep us company; they are also advising us on our lives. Later, that young brother confessed the whole thing in his small group. His leader didn’t scold him, but went with him to correct the expense reports, and encouraged him to keep loving those coworkers while standing firm in his values. He said, “I still eat with them. It’s just that now I know who’s helping me make my life decisions.”
lessons.light: Self-centered people like to hear what pleases them, so they choose companions who make them comfortable. Selfless people are willing to hear the truth, because they want Jesus to reign, not their own preferences. The Bible is my standard: I weigh a friend’s advice not by whether it sounds pleasant, but by whether it fits God’s heart.
think: Why did Rehoboam reject the old men’s advice and follow the young men’s counsel?
When I make important decisions, whose opinions do I listen to most? Where are they taking me?
What matter this week do I need to bring to a godly, mature person for advice?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often choose to listen to voices that make me comfortable, and I assume I won’t be influenced. Forgive my self-deception. Help me discern the advice around me and let the Bible be my standard. Give me courage to love my coworkers and friends while standing firm in my values, not drifting with the current. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, about a decision you are weighing, take the initiative to seek advice from an older, godly mentor or spiritual companion who is more mature than you. Share your thoughts honestly and listen to their counsel.
lessons.quick: Friends don’t just share your meals; they’re advising you on your life.
text: King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men who had stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, saying, “What counsel do you give me to answer these people?”
They replied, “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever.”
But he abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him, who stood before him.
He said to them, “What counsel do you give, that we may answer these people who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Make the yoke that your father put on us lighter’?”

The young men who had grown up with him said to him, “Tell these people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter to us’—tell them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.
Now my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.’”
So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king asked, saying, “Come to me again the third day.”
The king answered the people roughly, and abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him,

and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”

lessons.title: A Friend Who Won’t Let Go
lessons.hear:
This week isn’t only about choosing friends; it’s even more about becoming one. The Bible tells a moving story of loyalty between a young widow and her elderly mother-in-law. Naomi had lost her husband and both her sons. She decided to return to her homeland and urged her two daughters-in-law to go back to their own families. Orpah tearfully said goodbye, “but Ruth stayed with her” (Ruth 1:14).

Ruth said, “Where you go, I will go; and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16). This was a commitment with nothing to gain. Naomi was old, poor, and bitter—she even asked people to call her “Mara,” which means “bitter” (see Ruth 1:20). Ruth didn’t choose someone who could benefit her; she chose the person who most needed a friend.

Proverbs says, “A man of many companions may be ruined, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24). We often ask, “Where can I find a friend like that?” But God invites us to ask first, “Can I become a friend like that?” Many people lament that they have no close friends, yet they rarely commit themselves to anyone. Friendship is like a garden: it doesn’t grow on its own. Someone has to water it, pull the weeds, and tend it day by day.

Today’s practice: choose a “Naomi” in your life. It may be an older person who has just lost a spouse, an old classmate going through a low season, a coworker who has moved to a new city, or the person at church who always sits alone. You don’t need to promise a lifetime at the start, but you can take one concrete step of loyalty: a regular weekly check-in, a monthly meal together, or showing up when they need you. Use wisdom and appropriate boundaries too: when caring for someone of the opposite sex or someone in financial trouble, it’s best to involve your family or small group. Ruth’s loyalty was later written into David’s family tree. Your faithfulness to one person today may become a page in God’s great story.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 stands for every person connected to me—and Ruth chose the one who was least valued. Selfless friendship doesn’t ask, “What can this person give me?” but “Who most needs a friend?” Self-denial—for Jesus, for others, not for myself—this kind of friendship is what God’s kingdom looks like on earth.
think: In Ruth 1:16-17, what commitments did Ruth make to Naomi?
Am I waiting for others to become good friends to me, or am I becoming a good friend to others first?
Who is the “Naomi” in my life, and what concrete act of loyalty can I offer?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the friend who sticks closer than a brother and never leaves me. Make me not only someone who looks for good friends, but someone willing to be a good friend to others. Open my eyes to see the Naomi beside me, and give me Ruth’s loyalty and wisdom to be with them when they need it most. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone who most needs a friend and settle on a regular way to care for them—such as a weekly message or a monthly meal—and do it for the first time this week.
lessons.quick: Rather than waiting for a good friend, become a good friend first.
text: They lifted up their voices and wept again; then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth stayed with her.
She said, “Behold, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her god. Follow your sister-in-law.”
Ruth said, “Don’t urge me to leave you, and to return from following you, for where you go, I will go; and where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.
Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD do so to me, and more also, if anything but death parts you and me.”
When Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she stopped urging her.

lessons.title: Wake Up, Don’t Be Deceived
lessons.hear:
Some in the Corinthian church had been influenced by the ideas around them and had begun to doubt the resurrection of the dead. Paul quoted a popular saying of the day: “If the dead are not raised, then ‘let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’” (1 Corinthians 15:32). Then he warned, “Don’t be deceived! ‘Evil companionships corrupt good morals’” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Today, use these words to take an honest look at your own “circle of friends.” The companions who influence us today aren’t only the friends we see in person; they include the influencers we follow, the short videos we scroll through every day, the group chats we belong to, and the shows and podcasts we listen to. Every day they speak to us: “Live for the moment.” “If it feels right, do it.” “Faith is so old-fashioned.” Without our noticing, our values get rearranged. The self-deception Paul talks about is assuming we are immune.

Peter is an example of someone carried away by his surroundings without realizing it. On the night Jesus was arrested, “When they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and had sat down together, Peter sat among them” (Luke 22:55). He sat down among people who didn’t know Jesus, wanting to keep warm and not be recognized. And right there by that fire, he said, “I don’t know him” (Luke 22:57). But that wasn’t the end of the story. The risen Lord later restored him personally beside another charcoal fire (see John 21:9-17).

So the way to adjust isn’t to cut off every unbelieving friend in one stroke. It involves three things. First, wake up: see honestly who is shaping you. Second, adjust: reduce the input that pulls you away from God—for example, unfollow certain accounts, or try the app’s digital Sabbath. Third, add: deliberately spend more time with godly friends. Paul concludes: “Wake up righteously and don’t sin, for some have no knowledge of God” (1 Corinthians 15:34). We wake up not to escape the world, but to become people in the world who help others come to know God.
lessons.light: Assuming I can’t be influenced is itself a kind of pride. Humble people admit they can be shaped, so they carefully choose the voices that shape them. Our focus is on Jesus—not on influencers, and not on which way the group chat is blowing. Change begins with me: first I adjust what I take in, then I influence those around me.
think: When Paul says “Don’t be deceived,” what were the Corinthian believers deceiving themselves about?
Among the accounts and groups I follow, which ones are quietly changing my values?
Which source of influence will I cancel, reduce, or add today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often think I can’t be influenced, yet without noticing I have sat down by a fire far from you. Thank you that you still restore the fallen beside a charcoal fire. Wake me up to righteousness, help me see clearly who is shaping me, and give me courage to adjust, so that among people I become someone who helps them know you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, review the accounts you follow and the groups you’re in, and unfollow one account that pulls you away from God. Then arrange to share a meal or pray with a godly friend this week.
lessons.quick: Thinking you can’t be influenced is the greatest self-deception of all.
text: Why do we also stand in jeopardy every hour?
I affirm, by the boasting in you which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily.
If I fought with animals at Ephesus for human purposes, what does it profit me? If the dead are not raised, then “let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
