Don’t be deceived! “Evil companionships corrupt good morals.”
Wake up righteously and don’t sin, for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

lessons.title: Becoming Someone’s Wise Companion
lessons.hear:
This week’s memory verse is: “One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm” (Proverbs 13:20). Reading it, we easily think only, “I need to find wise friends.” But try turning the verse around: Am I the “wise man” beside someone else? Who will grow wiser by walking with me?

The same chapter of Proverbs says, “The teaching of the wise is a spring of life, to turn from the snares of death” (Proverbs 13:14). It also says, “A trustworthy envoy gains healing” (Proverbs 13:17). Wisdom isn’t a degree or a gift for words; it is fearing God, being teachable, and living what you say. A person with that kind of life is like a spring: whoever drinks from it finds life.

This week we have seen that friends shape our direction; that Rehoboam lost most of his kingdom by listening to the wrong companions; that Ruth became a blessing to another through her loyalty; and we have honestly examined who is shaping us. Now it’s time to pass on what we’ve received.

The most natural way to multiply is to become a companion to a young person, a newcomer, or a new believer. Think about it: Is there a young person at church just starting out in the working world, still choosing their circle of friends? Is there someone who has just arrived and hasn’t found a community yet? You don’t have to be perfect. You only need to be willing to walk part of the road with them: share meals, listen to their worries, and tell them about the times you went the wrong way and God brought you back. Today, invite someone to walk with you, and share with them what you received this week: “We’re all shaped by our friends, so let’s be friends who bring each other closer to God.”
lessons.light: The “3” in 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children. Multiplication isn’t making copies of a perfect me; it’s letting God’s wisdom flow through me to the next person. Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart: the Spirit will point out the person who needs a companion, and as you walk together, he will be the true wisdom among you.
think: In Proverbs 13:14-20, how do the outcomes of the wise and the foolish differ?
Who would grow closer to God by walking with me? Am I that kind of person?
Which young person or newcomer will I invite to walk part of the road with me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for the wise companions you placed around me who have shaped my life. Make me a wise companion to others as well, bringing them life like a spring. Show me the person who needs someone to walk with them, and let us walk together in your ways. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a young person or newcomer at church and invite them to a meal this week. Listen to how they’re doing, and share a time when a friend led you toward God.
lessons.quick: Don’t just look for the wise—become a wise companion to someone else.
text: The teaching of the wise is a spring of life, to turn from the snares of death.
Good understanding wins favor, but the way of the unfaithful is hard.
Every prudent man acts from knowledge, but a fool exposes folly.
A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a trustworthy envoy gains healing.
Poverty and shame come to him who refuses discipline, but he who heeds correction shall be honored.
Longing fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but fools detest turning from evil.
One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm.

weeks.keyText: One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm.

weeks.title: Friendship in Crisis and Repair
weeks.theme: Even the best friendships crack; covering offenses and taking the first step to repair can turn the breach into a deeper bond.
group: Read Acts 15:36-41 and 2 Timothy 4:11. How did the relationship between Paul, Barnabas, and Mark change over time?
Do you have a friendship that faded because of a misunderstanding or an argument? What has kept you from repairing it?
Toward which friend are you willing to take the first step of repair this week, and what concrete action will you take?
weeks.sunday: This weekend, spend fifteen quiet minutes praying about a friendship that has cracked, handing over to God both the other person’s name and your own share of responsibility. If the timing is right and it is safe, invite them for tea somewhere public and relaxed, and begin by apologizing for your part. If it isn’t yet right to meet, start by mailing them a greeting card. Afterward, thank God for his protection, and ask a companion to pray with you.

lessons.title: They Separated from Each Other
lessons.hear:
Paul and Barnabas were one of the most moving ministry partnerships in the early church. When Paul had just come to faith and all the disciples were afraid of him, it was Barnabas who “took him and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:27). They taught together in Antioch, went on the first missionary journey together, and faced death together. Yet even friends like these had a falling-out.

The spark was Mark. Barnabas wanted to take Mark along again, but Paul refused, because Mark had left them partway through the previous journey. The text is very honest: “Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39). Scripture doesn’t cover up the flaws of these two spiritual giants, and it doesn’t clearly declare who was right and who was wrong. Perhaps Paul prioritized the mission, while Barnabas prioritized giving someone a second chance. Both had good reasons, and both had their limits.

This brings us great comfort. A friendship in crisis doesn’t mean you aren’t spiritual, and it doesn’t mean the relationship is worthless. Even the best friends are two imperfect people; even the sturdiest house develops cracks that need repair. What matters isn’t whether there are cracks, but how we face them.

This week’s memory verse says: “He who covers an offense promotes love; but he who repeats a matter separates best friends” (Proverbs 17:9). “Covering” doesn’t mean hiding sin or enabling harm. It means not broadcasting a friend’s weaknesses, not dredging up old grievances, and not letting one conflict define a whole friendship. God even used this separation: Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus, and Paul took Silas to strengthen the churches, so the gospel actually went further. And the story isn’t over—this week we will follow it all the way to repair.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. A friendship crisis is often not about one person being entirely right and the other entirely wrong, but about two people each holding their ground and refusing to yield. Letting Jesus reign means acknowledging that this relationship is in his hands, not in my verdict of right and wrong.
think: What did Paul and Barnabas each insist on, and what were their reasons?
Do I treat a crack in a friendship as proof that “this relationship has failed”?
In a friendship that has cracked, what can I “cover” today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you know that we are all imperfect, and even the best friendships crack. Thank you that even when Paul and Barnabas parted ways, you were still in control. Keep me from broadcasting my friends’ weaknesses or dredging up old grievances, and prepare a path to repair in my cracked friendships. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray for a friendship that has cracked, and decide that this week you will not talk about that friend’s faults in front of anyone.
lessons.quick: A crack isn’t failure; what matters is how you face it.
text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

lessons.title: If He Comes to You, Receive Him
lessons.hear:
Two close friends from college went into business together after graduation and opened a small shop. Later they had a bitter falling-out over splitting profits and how to run the business. The shop closed, they blocked each other everywhere, and they even made sure to attend class reunions at different times. Ten years later, one of them heard at church that we should “repair relationships,” and he scoffed inside: “Once you’ve fallen out, you’ve fallen out. There’s no going back.”

This is an old mindset many people hold: once a friendship breaks, it’s like a shattered cup that can never be glued back together. Leaving the group chat, blocking the person, becoming strangers—this seems to be the “cleanest” grown-up way to handle it.

But look at what happened next with Mark. The young man who had once split Paul and Barnabas reappears years later in Paul’s letters. Writing from prison to the church in Colossae, Paul made a point of saying: “Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received instructions, ‘if he comes to you, receive him’)” (Colossians 4:10). Paul had not only reconciled with Mark; he was vouching for him. At the very end of his life, Paul wrote: “Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). The one once judged “not to be taken along” became the one who was “useful to me.”

This is God’s perspective: in Christ, a break is not necessarily the end. People grow, wounds heal, and God works in both hearts. Of course, repair takes time, and it takes two. Some relationships involve ongoing harm or deception and require boundaries. But many broken friendships are simply waiting for one person to speak first. Later, as that brother prayed, he was struck by the words in Colossians 4:10: “receive him.” He unblocked his old friend and sent a message: “It’s been a long time. How have you been? About what happened back then—I was in the wrong too.” Two days later, the reply came: “I’ve been wanting to say I’m sorry to you all this time.”
lessons.light: Paul’s journey from “don’t take him” to “useful to me” is a testimony to changing a mindset: information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, adjustment… God changed not only Mark but also the way Paul saw Mark. Change begins with me: when I first change how I see the other person, new possibilities open for the relationship.
think: How did Paul’s view of Mark change over time?
Is there someone in my heart about whom I’ve decided, “Once we fell out, there’s no going back”?
What simple way can I use to show goodwill to that friend?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for restoring Mark after his failure and for changing the way Paul saw him. I confess there are people in my heart I long ago decided I “can’t go back to.” Soften my heart, make me willing to speak first, and give me wisdom to discern which relationships need repair and which need boundaries. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a friend you have blocked or drifted away from, and pray for them. If you are sure it is safe, send them a simple greeting—there’s no need to rush into explaining the past.
lessons.quick: In Christ, a break is not necessarily the end.
text: All my affairs will be made known to you by Tychicus, the beloved brother, faithful servant, and fellow bondservant in the Lord.
I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that he may know your circumstances and comfort your hearts,
together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is going on here.
Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received instructions, “if he comes to you, receive him”),
and Jesus who is called Justus. These are my only fellow workers for God’s Kingdom who are of the circumcision, men who have been a comfort to me.

lessons.title: Thinking the Same Way in the Lord
lessons.hear:
Philippians is a letter full of joy, yet near the end Paul names two women: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). Who were they? Paul says that “they labored with me in the Good News” (Philippians 4:3). These were two co-workers who had once served side by side, but a rift had opened between them—serious enough that the whole church knew about it.

Notice how Paul handles it. First, he doesn’t air the details of their dispute in the letter. He covers it, simply urging them to think the same way in the Lord. Their unity isn’t based on agreeing about everything, but on both being in the Lord. Second, he asks a third party to help: “Yes, I beg you also, true partner, help these women” (Philippians 4:3). Repairing a friendship sometimes requires someone both sides trust to walk alongside them. Third, he lifts their eyes: “Rejoice in the Lord always! … Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand” (Philippians 4:4-5). In the light of eternity, many quarrels don’t seem so important anymore.

Today’s practice is to take one small step toward repair. If you are one of the people involved, start by apologizing for your part—without adding “but you also…” A simple “I spoke too harshly last time, and I’m sorry” often carries more power than ten pages of explanation. If you’re an onlooker and see a rift between two friends, you can be that “true partner”: don’t take sides, don’t pass messages back and forth, pray for each of them separately, and when the time is right, gently encourage them to reconcile.

Remember too that repair doesn’t have to happen all at once. Maybe today it’s just a greeting, and next month it’s tea together. Maybe it will take help from a pastor or counselor. Reconciliation takes two; what you are responsible for is your own step.
lessons.light: Gentleness and yielding mean laying down power and returning to our proper place. What Euodia and Syntyche needed was not to prove who was right, but to remember again that they belonged to the same Lord. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than being right. When I am willing to let go first, I leave room for the Holy Spirit to work.
think: How did Paul handle the rift between Euodia and Syntyche?
In a cracked friendship, what part of the responsibility is mine?
What small step can I take today—an apology, a greeting, or praying as a go-between?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the Lord who makes peace. I confess that I often wait for the other person to apologize first, or I only want to prove I’m not wrong. Give me a gentle, yielding heart to own my part first. And when I am an onlooker, make me a true partner who doesn’t pass on gossip or take sides, but helps my friends be of one mind in you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, offer a friend you have a rift with an unconditional apology for your part; or pray separately for two friends who are at odds and look for a chance to gently encourage them.
lessons.quick: Repair begins with my own step—no “but” attached.
text: Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved.
I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.
Yes, I beg you also, true partner, help these women, for they labored with me in the Good News with Clement also, and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.

lessons.title: Three Questions by the Charcoal Fire
lessons.hear:
Peter had been one of Jesus’ closest friends, yet on that most critical night, beside a charcoal fire, he denied knowing him three times. This is the deepest wound a friendship can suffer: not an attack from a stranger, but betrayal by a friend.

How did the risen Jesus repair this relationship? Once again he made a charcoal fire, this time on the shore, and prepared breakfast. When they had eaten, he asked Peter three times, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” (John 21:16). Three denials, three questions about love. Jesus didn’t pretend it hadn’t happened, nor did he list Peter’s failures one by one. In a gentle yet honest way, he let the wound be seen and let love be spoken again. Peter was grieved: “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you” (John 21:17). Then Jesus entrusted his sheep to him, trusted him again, and said, “Follow me” (John 21:19).

This scene is a mirror for examining ourselves. First, when I have hurt a friend, do I face it as Peter did, or do I keep avoiding it and pretend nothing happened, hoping time will wash it all away? Repair requires honestly saying, “I hurt you, and I’m sorry.” Second, when a friend has hurt me, do I, like Jesus, take the initiative to light the charcoal fire, or do I wait for them to come begging on their knees? Jesus was the one who had been wounded, yet he was the one who took the first step.

Wisdom matters here too. Jesus restored Peter after Peter was genuinely sorry. If a friendship involves ongoing manipulation, deception, or harm, real change needs to be seen before repair; keeping your distance or seeking help when necessary does not go against love. But for most friendships wounded by weakness, misunderstanding, or careless words, ask yourself today: Am I Peter, who needs to go and apologize, or am I the one who needs to light the fire first?
lessons.light: Self-centered people want the other person to back down first when they’ve been hurt, and refuse to face it when they’ve done the hurting. Selfless people learn from Jesus: when hurt, they prepare the charcoal fire first; when they hurt others, they honestly admit their wrong. Jesus is my example: he repaired the relationship not by denying the wound, but by healing it with love and saying once more, “Follow me.”
think: Why did Jesus ask Peter three times? How did he rebuild his trust in Peter?
In a wounded friendship, am I more like Peter, who needs to apologize, or the one who needs to light the fire first?
How will I honestly face the situation, or reach out with an invitation to that friend, today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, like Peter I have failed you, yet beside the charcoal fire you restored me. When I hurt a friend, help me honestly admit my wrong instead of hiding. When a friend hurts me, help me take the first step as you did. Give me the wisdom to discern when to repair and when I first need to protect myself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, if you have hurt a friend, take the initiative to acknowledge it specifically and apologize. If you are the one who was hurt, pray for them and then invite them to breakfast or coffee.
lessons.quick: Jesus was wounded yet lit the fire first; Peter had wounded and faced it honestly.
text: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”

lessons.title: The Bond of Perfection
lessons.hear:
Paul’s words to the Colossian church are like a set of clothes tailor-made for friendship: “Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance” (Colossians 3:12). Then he says: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (Colossians 3:13).

Paul is very realistic. He knows that complaints will arise between people. He doesn’t say, “Good Christians never argue”; he says “if any man has a complaint,” then bear with one another and forgive. Then comes a beautiful line: “Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14). Love is like a belt that ties all the virtues together—and like thread that stitches torn fabric back together. Where it has been mended, a mark of love remains.

Over these five weeks we have traveled the journey of friendship together. Jesus calls us friends, befriends sinners, and weeps with those who weep. Jonathan used a covenant to help David fulfill his calling. Friends are like iron sharpening iron, shaping one another into the likeness of Christ. We choose our friends carefully and resolve to be good friends to others. And finally, we have learned to face the cracks and take the first step toward repair. “He who covers an offense promotes love” (Proverbs 17:9)—this is the secret of lasting friendship.

Today, go over everything you have received along the way once more, and pass it on. Find a friend and tell them: “These past few weeks I’ve learned that true friendship isn’t friendship without cracks; it’s friendship that gets mended again and again in Christ.” You can also open the 920 Relationship Map in the app, add a card for this friend, and write down how you are praying for them. “Let the peace of God rule in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15), and your circle of friends will become a corner of God’s kingdom on earth.
lessons.light: The “9” in 920 is the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit, and love is the thread that binds all the fruit together. Letting God’s peace rule in our hearts means letting Jesus reign. As our friendships are mended again and again in him, we are building God’s system, and people can see heaven’s love lived out on earth.
think: In Colossians 3:12-14, what “clothes” does Paul list, and what role does love play among them?
Of all I learned about friendship over these five weeks, what has touched me most deeply?
With which friend will I share what I’ve received, and how?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for forgiving me in Christ and for mending me with your love. Help me put on compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance, and above all walk in love, the bond of perfection. Let your peace rule in my heart, and make my friendships a sign of your kingdom. May all glory be yours. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, add a card for a friend in the app’s 920 Relationship Map and write down your prayer for them. Then send them a message sharing one thing you’ve learned about friendship over these weeks.
lessons.quick: Love is the thread that stitches broken friendships back together.
text: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

weeks.keyText: He who covers an offense promotes love; but he who repeats a matter separates best friends.

weeks.title: Who Is My Neighbor?
weeks.theme: Love doesn’t draw a circle and ask who qualifies; it steps outside the circle to become someone’s neighbor.
group: In the story of the Good Samaritan, which of his actions moves you most, and why?
Can you share a time you “passed by on the other side,” or a time a stranger came near and helped you?
Which neighbor do you want to be a neighbor to this week, and what specifically do you plan to do?
weeks.sunday: Prepare a small box of fruit or snacks, and during the day go with your family to knock on the door of a neighbor you don’t yet know well. Briefly introduce yourselves, ask how they’re doing, and don’t stay long. Before you go, pray for that household and ask the Lord to prepare both your hearts; when you get home, give thanks together for the encounter and write down their names, so that next time you see them you can greet them by name and keep the friendship going.

lessons.title: Go and Be a Neighbor
lessons.hear:
The expert in the law asked a very “safe” question: Who is my neighbor? Jesus answered with a story, then turned the question around at the end: “Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” (Luke 10:36). The lawyer wanted to know where the boundary of love was drawn. Jesus wanted him to see that love isn’t about drawing circles at all—it’s about going out.

In the story, the priest and the Levite both “saw” the wounded man, yet each “passed by on the other side.” They weren’t necessarily bad men. Maybe they were hurrying to serve at the temple, maybe they were afraid of becoming ceremonially unclean, maybe they worried the robbers were still nearby. We’re good at finding reasons too: I’m too tired today, I don’t really know him, I don’t want trouble. The real difference isn’t in the seeing but in where the heart moves after we see. The Samaritan “saw him” and “was moved with compassion” (Luke 10:33), and then comes a whole string of verbs: he went to him, poured on oil and wine, bandaged his wounds, set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, took care of him, paid the bill, and promised to come back. Love grew feet, hands—and a wallet.

Most surprising of all, the hero is a Samaritan—an “outsider” in Jewish eyes. When the beaten man came to, he probably discovered that the one who saved him was someone he would never normally greet. God often tears down the walls in our hearts this way.

The deepest layer of this story is Jesus himself. We are the ones lying by the roadside, half dead. He came down from heaven, came right up to us, paid the price, and promised to come again. “The Word became flesh and lived among us” (John 1:14)—he is the first neighbor who ever came near to us. So “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10:37) is not a heavy moral command; it’s the natural response of someone who has been loved.

A neighbor isn’t simply someone who lives nearby; it’s someone I’m willing to draw near to. Today, may the Holy Spirit open our eyes and move our hearts.
lessons.light: The lawyer’s question was self-centered: first pin down the limits of my responsibility so I can look justified. Selfless love doesn’t ask, “Whom do I have to love?” but, “Who needs me to become their neighbor?” This is a change of viewpoint—from starting in my own comfort zone to starting from the heart of Jesus. Once the mindset changes, our steps follow.
think: After the Samaritan “was moved with compassion,” what specific actions did he take?
What reasons do I most often use to “pass by on the other side”?
Who is lying by the “roadside” of my life this week, needing me to take one step closer?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for coming near to me when I was most broken and for paying the price for me. Forgive me for so often seeing and then walking around, wanting only to draw the line of my responsibility. Holy Spirit, open my eyes and soften my heart, so that today I’ll be willing to draw near to someone in need and be their neighbor. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: As you go out or head to work today, watch for a coworker who is alone, an older person struggling to carry something, or a lost traveler. Stop and ask, “Can I help?”—and then really lend a hand.
lessons.quick: A neighbor isn’t someone who lives nearby, but someone I’m willing to draw near to.
text: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.title: Asking the Wrong Question
lessons.hear:
One brother lived in the same apartment building for more than ten years, yet he couldn’t name a single person he saw in the elevator every day. He liked to say, “That’s city life. Everyone minds their own business—not bothering each other is the polite thing.” Then one winter night an ambulance pulled up outside, and he learned that the elderly man who lived alone across the hall had collapsed at home and lain there for quite some time. He couldn’t sleep that night. “I walked past his door every day,” he said, “and I never once knocked.”

Many of us carry an old mindset: neighbors come with boundaries. People who live close, people we get along with, people in the same church or the same group chat—they count. Everyone outside the circle is “none of my business.” The lawyer thought the same way. He actually knew the answer: love “your neighbor as yourself” (Luke 10:27). But, “desiring to justify himself,” he pressed Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). Underneath that question hid another one: Who is not my neighbor? If I can just draw the circle a little smaller, I can declare that I’ve passed the test.

God’s perspective is completely different. Already in the Law, God drew the circle wide: “The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34). Jesus went further, turning the question from “Who deserves my love?” into “Whose neighbor am I willing to become?” The first puts me at the center; the second puts the other person there.

This doesn’t mean carrying the burdens of an entire city. We can’t take care of everyone, but we can stop ruling anyone out in advance. Love doesn’t begin with a list; it begins with an unguarded heart.

That brother began greeting people in the elevator and writing down his neighbors’ names. Six months later, when a foreign caregiver from upstairs was quietly crying in the hallway, he was the first to stop and ask what was wrong. “I didn’t become a more enthusiastic person,” he said. “I just stopped pretending not to see.”
lessons.light: “Who is my neighbor?” is a question of the head—calculating responsibility and protecting myself. “Whose neighbor can I become?” is a question of the heart—following the heartbeat of Jesus. Living from the head breeds worry: fear of hassle, fear of being taken advantage of. Living from the heart brings joy: in love we discover encounters God has already arranged. Change your viewpoint, and you change your mindset.
think: Why did the lawyer press Jesus with the question “Who is my neighbor?”
Do I keep a mental list of people I “don’t have to love”? Who is on it?
Which “outsider” can I bring back into view this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, your love never draws small circles. Forgive me for so often wanting to prove myself right and quietly shutting some people out of the reach of my love. Enlarge my heart, so that I stop asking who deserves my love and start asking whose neighbor I can become—drawing near to others just as Jesus drew near to me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down one household on your floor or your street whose names you don’t yet know. When you see them today or tomorrow, greet them first, introduce yourself, and ask what they like to be called.
lessons.quick: Don’t ask “Who is my neighbor?” Ask “Whose neighbor can I become?”
text: Behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?”
He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”
He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”
But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?”

lessons.title: It Starts with a Name
lessons.hear:
Loving your neighbor sounds big, but it often begins in very small places. God’s instructions to Israel in Leviticus are remarkably down-to-earth: don’t show partiality, don’t go around as a slanderer, don’t hate your brother in your heart. Then comes the summary: “You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:18). How we treat our neighbor turns out to be how we respond to God.

In today’s cities, the first step in loving a neighbor is often simply letting that person stop being “the guy next door” and become someone with a name. You can start like this. 1. See: notice the people you brush past every day—the cleaning lady, the building security guard, the owner of the breakfast shop downstairs, the immigrant family that just moved in. 2. Greet: a “good morning,” a smile, a “What should I call you?”—and then remember, so you can use their name next time. 3. Serve in small ways: hold the elevator, collect a package for a neighbor who’s traveling, give a heads-up before a typhoon.

A sister who moved from Southeast Asia to Taiwan for work said the warmest moment after moving into her new community was when the building manager called her by name on her third day. A name is a small door; someone who is called by name feels seen.

Of course, drawing near also takes wisdom and good judgment. You don’t need to rush to invite a brand-new acquaintance into your home or exchange every bit of contact information right away. When it comes to being alone with someone of the opposite sex, knocking on doors late at night, or lending money, it’s better to go slower and keep things more public. Love isn’t reckless; it’s gentle, steady goodwill.

Paul wrote, “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:4). Today, start looking to the things of others—beginning with one name.
lessons.light: Calling someone by name brings them from the “background” into the “foreground.” The self-centered remember only the names that are useful to them; the selfless remember every person God has placed around them. The “2” in 920—every person I am connected to—starts with these people we pass every day but have never really seen.
think: What “shall nots” does Leviticus 19:15-18 use to protect one’s neighbor?
Who are the people I see every day but whose names I don’t know?
What small act of service can I do for a neighbor today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you know my name, and you see the people I pass by and overlook every day. Give me an attentive heart, the courage to smile and greet, and the care to remember people’s names. Give me wisdom and good judgment too, so that I keep doing good within safe boundaries. May my neighbors feel your warmth through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, greet someone you see every day but whose name you don’t know (a security guard, a cleaner, the neighbor next door) and ask their name. Tonight, write it down and pray a sentence for them.
lessons.quick: Loving my neighbor starts with calling one person by name.
text: “‘You shall do no injustice in judgment. You shall not be partial to the poor, nor show favoritism to the great; but you shall judge your neighbor in righteousness.
“‘You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people. “‘You shall not endanger the life of your neighbor. I am the LORD.
“‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.
“‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.

lessons.title: Disciples Who Wanted Fire
lessons.hear:
When a Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus, James and John flared up at once: “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them, just as Elijah did?” (Luke 9:54). They had even found a biblical precedent for their anger. But Jesus turned and rebuked them: “For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them” (Luke 9:56).

Few of us actually want to call down fire, but small flames in the heart are common enough: the resident who is always complaining in the community group chat, the neighbor who leaves trash bags piled at my door, the person who opposes everything at the homeowners’ association meeting, the immigrant family with a different accent and “strange” habits. We may not attack them, but inside we “burn them up”—we stop greeting them, mention them to others with a touch of sarcasm, or simply act as if they don’t exist.

That is the self-centered life: if you won’t welcome me, I don’t have to love you anymore; if you offend my standards, I have the right to withdraw my goodwill.

But the most beautiful thing about the gospel is that people who fail can be restored. Years later, this same John who once wanted to burn up a Samaritan village was sent with Peter to Samaria to pray for the new believers there, and on the way back they “preached the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans” (Acts 8:25). On the same soil, he went from wanting to bring down the fire of judgment to bringing the good news. What changed him wasn’t self-reproach but a long time spent with Jesus, slowly being reshaped by his heart that came “to save.”

Today, examine yourself honestly: Is there a “Samaritan” in my heart? The first step of adjustment isn’t forcing yourself to like that person right away. It is admitting the fire, handing it over to Jesus, and asking him for one small chance to replace indifference with kindness. If a neighbor’s behavior has crossed into harassment or threats, take it to the building management or the proper authorities. Not calling down fire doesn’t mean not setting boundaries.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power—God’s power to decide who deserves love and who deserves punishment. When James and John wanted to call down fire on God’s behalf, they were stepping out of place. Humility is returning to our proper place as human beings: letting God be the Judge while I am only a servant of love. When the selfless are rejected, they can calmly go on “to another village” without leaving in a rage.
think: How did Jesus respond to his disciples’ anger? What was his heart?
Is there a neighbor or group I secretly want to “call down fire” on?
What small kindness could replace my coldness toward them?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you didn’t come to destroy people but to save them. I confess that I hold anger and contempt toward some of my neighbors, and I even make excuses for my coldness. Forgive me for stepping out of place to judge. Renew my heart with yours, change me as you changed John, and keep me gentle even when I am rejected. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of the neighbor or resident you’d most like to “burn up,” and pray for them quietly today. Next time you see them, nod and say hello first—without sarcasm—and don’t talk about them behind their back.
lessons.quick: Jesus came to save, so I’ll stop calling down fire in my heart.
text: It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem
and sent messengers before his face. They went and entered into a village of the Samaritans, so as to prepare for him.
They didn’t receive him, because he was traveling with his face set toward Jerusalem.
When his disciples, James and John, saw this, they said, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky and destroy them, just as Elijah did?”
But he turned and rebuked them, “You don’t know of what kind of spirit you are.
For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them.” They went to another village.

lessons.title: Bring Your Neighbors to Prayer
lessons.hear:
This week we’ve walked from the lawyer’s question onto the Samaritan’s road, and then turned back to see the walls in our own hearts. Finally, let’s return to the source of it all: what kind of God our God is. Moses said that the LORD is Lord of lords, yet “He executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner in giving him food and clothing” (Deuteronomy 10:18). Then comes the next line: “Therefore love the foreigner, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).

That “therefore” matters. Israel was to love foreigners not because they were naturally warmhearted but because they remembered living under someone else’s roof, and God had loved them first. It’s the same for us. We were once spiritual outsiders, far from God; Jesus came near and made us members of God’s household. When we remember that we have been loved, loving our neighbor is no longer a performance—it’s a response to grace.

Good habits take root through repetition. This week can be boiled down to three sentences: Love isn’t drawing circles; it’s drawing near. Drawing near starts with calling someone by name. When you’re rejected, hand your anger over to Jesus. Put those three sentences in your phone’s notes and read them each day before you head out.

The life of the gospel is also meant to multiply. One person drawing near to a neighbor is a single lamp; a group drawing near together is a whole street lit up. You could invite a brother or sister to pray with you for your building or street, each of you adopting a few households, reminding each other and sharing stories. Or tell this week’s story to your children and take them with you to thank the building manager.

Loving your neighbor isn’t a one-time act of heroism but a way of life. When many ordinary people draw near to one another in small things every day, the kingdom of God quietly comes to one little lane.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry: a life loved by God naturally overflows in love for neighbors, and one person’s love, through companions, multiplies into a group’s service. That is how we build God’s system—not by starting with big events, but by remembering grace and reminding one another.
think: In Deuteronomy 10:17-19, what reason does God give for loving the foreigner?
Do I still remember that I too was once a “foreigner”?
Which companion will I invite this week to pray with me for our neighborhood?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you are Lord of lords, yet you stoop down to the fatherless, the widow, and the foreigner. Thank you for loving me when I was far from you. Help me always remember this grace, bring my neighbors before you one by one, and shine together with my companions as a light on this street. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: In the app’s Relationship Map, add a card for a neighbor you met this week and write a prayer for them. Then text a brother or sister and invite them to pray with you for your community for five minutes this week.
lessons.quick: When I remember I’ve been loved, I’ll draw near to others.
text: For the LORD your God, he is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons or take bribes.
He executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner in giving him food and clothing.
Therefore love the foreigner, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

weeks.keyText: Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”

weeks.title: Welcoming Strangers with Love
weeks.theme: Hospitality opens the door of our home and, even more, the door of our heart; it needn’t be perfect—just a sincere seat saved for someone.
group: Who has welcomed you into their home? What detail of that welcome has stayed with you?
When it comes to hosting, what is my biggest worry—my home, my cooking, my time, or the fear of awkwardness?
Which stranger (a newcomer, a single person, an international student, someone who lives alone) do you want to welcome this week, and how?
weeks.sunday: Invite a newcomer, an international student, or a friend who lives alone to share a simple meal at your home or a small restaurant nearby—a pot of noodle soup or a plate of dumplings is plenty. If your guest is of the opposite sex, have family members or roommates there too. Pray for your guest beforehand, and during the meal listen more than you talk. Afterward, give thanks for the meal, write down one need your guest mentioned, and check in on them next week.

lessons.title: Entertaining Angels Unaware
lessons.hear:
At the end of his letter, the author of Hebrews sounds like an old pastor giving last instructions to a child setting out on a long journey: “Let brotherly love continue. Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers” (Hebrews 13:1-2). The Greek word for hospitality literally means “love of strangers.” Brotherly love is loving our own; hospitality is reaching out in love to those who aren’t yet our own. The two stand side by side like the roots and branches of a tree: the roots go deep in God’s family, and the branches stretch out beyond the wall.

The author then adds a vivid line: “in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). His readers would likely have remembered Abraham welcoming three travelers at the door of his tent. That day he was simply doing what any hospitable person should do, yet without realizing it he welcomed messengers from God. You never know whether the weary young person at your dinner table tonight is someone God wants to comfort through you, or someone God wants to use to bless you.

Hospitality isn’t only opening the door; it is also remembering. The very next line says, “Remember those who are in bonds, as bound with them” (Hebrews 13:3). In the early church, Christians were often driven from their homes or thrown into prison for their faith. Brothers and sisters who opened their homes or brought food to the prisons often paid a price for it. Hospitality has never been an elegant social skill; it is a love willing to be present with others.

The deepest root of all is Jesus himself. He said, “I was a stranger and you took me in” (Matthew 25:35). When we welcome people, we are really welcoming the Lord—and we are able to welcome others only because the Lord first welcomed us wandering sinners. Before we open the doors of our homes, let’s ask him to open the doors of our hearts.
lessons.light: Hospitality is a kind of “making room”: giving up a little of my space, time, and plans for someone else. For the self-centered, the front door is a castle gate, welcoming only those who make them look good; for the selfless, it is a tent flap, ready to be lifted for anyone who is weary. When the focus shifts from “Is my home good enough?” to “Will they find rest here?” hospitality has begun.
think: What three kinds of love does Hebrews 13:1-3 place together, and how are they related?
Is my home more like a castle or a tent?
Who around me this month is like a “stranger” who needs a place?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you were once a stranger with nowhere to lay your head. Thank you for first welcoming me, a wanderer, and giving me a place in the Father’s house. Open the door of my heart, and open the door of my home, so that I never forget to show hospitality to strangers or to remember those who suffer. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone who recently moved, went abroad to study, or just started coming to church. Send them a message asking how they’re doing and whether they’d like help getting to know the area.
lessons.quick: Hospitality is loving strangers—first open your heart, then your home.
text: Let brotherly love continue.
Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.
Remember those who are in bonds, as bound with them, and those who are ill-treated, since you are also in the body.

lessons.title: A Bowl of Noodles Will Do
lessons.hear:
A sister working in the city lived in a tiny studio apartment. Whenever the church encouraged people to practice hospitality, she shook her head: “My place is too small and too messy, and I can’t cook. Inviting people over would just be embarrassing.” Then one night a young woman from her small group, freshly heartbroken after a breakup, texted that she didn’t want to be alone. The sister hesitated a long time before replying, “All I have is instant noodles and eggs. Do you want to come over?” That night the two of them sat on the edge of the bed eating noodles and talking late into the night. Six months later, the young woman shared in small group: “That bowl of instant noodles with an egg is my warmest memory of that whole winter.”

The old mindset in our hearts says hospitality comes with conditions: a big enough home, good enough food, a tidy enough house—otherwise, better not to. As a result, many front doors don’t open even once a year.

Look at Abraham. He lived in a tent, not a mansion. It was the heat of the day, and he was sitting at the tent door. As soon as he saw three strangers, “he ran to meet them from the tent door” and said, “I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart” (Genesis 18:2, 5). His hospitality began with a little water and a piece of bread. He did end up preparing a generous meal, but what moves us most is not the calf. It is his eagerness in running out, and his posture of service: “He stood by them under the tree, and they ate” (Genesis 18:8).

God’s perspective is that the heart of hospitality isn’t the venue but the intention; not performance but presence. Jesus said that even someone who gives “just a cup of cold water to drink” will not lose his reward (Matthew 10:42). You don’t need to be a Michelin-star chef—you just need to be willing to save a seat.

Of course, sincerity includes good judgment. If you live with roommates or family, talk it over first. With people you don’t know well, meet at a little place nearby. Between men and women, avoid being alone together indoors; bring another person along, which protects them and you. Sincere hospitality makes people feel both safe and warm.
lessons.light: Turning hospitality into a performance is self-centered—what matters is how others see my home. Treating hospitality as presence is selfless—what matters is whether the guest feels loved. The picture of Abraham “standing by them” shows the beauty of knowing one’s proper place: when the host doesn’t steal the show, the guests can rest.
think: When Abraham welcomed the strangers, which of his actions showed eagerness and humility?
Have I kept my door closed because things weren’t “perfect enough”?
What is the simplest way I could welcome someone this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that you didn’t wait for me to be perfect before you accepted me. Forgive me for so often turning hospitality into a performance and closing my door for fear of embarrassment. Give me Abraham’s eagerness to run out to meet people, along with wisdom and good judgment, so that with a bowl of noodles or a cup of tea others can experience your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, reach out to someone who has been feeling low or has just arrived somewhere new, and set up the simplest of meals together this week—cook a bowl of noodles at home, or treat them to one at a little place nearby.
lessons.quick: Hospitality needn’t be perfect—a bowl of noodles and a seat at the table are enough.
text: The LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day.
He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth,
and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant.
Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart. After that you may go your way, now that you have come to your servant.” They said, “Very well, do as you have said.”
Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three seahs of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”
Abraham ran to the herd, and fetched a tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it.
He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.

lessons.title: Hospitable Without Grumbling
lessons.hear:
Peter wrote to Christians scattered in many places and facing hard circumstances. He urged them, “above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves,” and immediately added, “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter 4:8-9). Peter was a practical man. He knew hospitality can be tiring, can cost money, and can upset our routines, so he specifically added “without grumbling.” Hospitality isn’t an occasional burst of enthusiasm; it’s a rhythm of life we can sustain.

How do we keep it going? Peter says, “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another” (1 Peter 4:10). Some people are good at cooking, some at conversation, some at decorating, and some are simply great at washing dishes. Hospitality doesn’t mean one person carries everything; it means each does their part according to the gifts God has given. If you can’t cook, you can be in charge of inviting. If your home is small, you can partner with a family that has a big living room. If you’re an introvert, you can greet guests at the door and remember their names.

You can start a simple hospitality plan today. 1. Choose a person: a new coworker, a newly arrived international student, an older person who lives alone, someone who has been missing from small group lately. 2. Choose a simple format: a home-cooked meal, a cup of coffee, a walk together, making dumplings together on the weekend. 3. Choose a safe arrangement: daytime or early evening, in a public place or with others present; no one-on-one time indoors between men and women, and no lending money.

You can write these three things down in the app’s Hospitality Plan, set a date, and pray for your guest beforehand. This isn’t about turning people into performance numbers; it simply keeps our good intentions from getting stuck at “Some other time.”

Finally, Peter says all this is so “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11). What your guests remember when they leave doesn’t need to be your cooking—just the sense of being valued and welcomed. That is exactly God’s heart.
lessons.light: “As each has received a gift” is the secret of selfless hospitality: you don’t have to force yourself to be good at everything, and you don’t have to compare yourself with others. When each of us acts as a good steward and offers what we have, a team’s hospitality becomes like an orchestra—many instruments blending into one song of welcome, with all the glory going to God.
think: In 1 Peter 4:8-11, how is hospitality related to loving one another and to spiritual gifts?
Where am I most likely to grumble when I host?
What part of hospitality can my gifts take on, and whom could I partner with?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for distributing all kinds of gifts among us. Help me to welcome others according to the gifts I’ve received—without comparing, without complaining, and without straining to prove myself. Lead me to choose a person, a time, and a safe way to host, so they can feel your welcome. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in the app’s Hospitality Plan, write down a person you want to welcome, a simple format, and a date—and send them an invitation the same day.
lessons.quick: When I host according to my gifts, I won’t grumble.
text: And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: Martha’s Kitchen
lessons.hear:
Martha was an enthusiastic host. When Jesus came to her village, “a certain woman named Martha received him into her house” (Luke 10:38). That was a wonderful start. But then the text says, “Martha was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). She rushed out of the kitchen, complained to Jesus about her sister, and even complained about the Lord himself: “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone?”

Many people who have hosted see themselves in Martha. Before the guests even arrive, we’re fretting that the floor isn’t shiny enough or there aren’t enough dishes. Once the guests sit down, we’re still dashing in and out of the kitchen with no time to hear a word they say. After they leave, we’re so exhausted that we snap at our family and secretly vow, “Never again.”

Martha’s problem wasn’t that she loved serving too much; it was that the focus of her serving had quietly shifted from people back to herself: Am I doing well enough? Why isn’t anyone helping me? Does the Lord even see how hard I’m working? Jesus gently said her name twice: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed” (Luke 10:41-42). He wasn’t rebuking her zeal; he was inviting her back to the center—first sit at the Lord’s feet, then step into the kitchen.

The good news is that this one failure didn’t define Martha. Later, at the time of Lazarus’s death, she made a clear confession of faith to Jesus (see John 11:27). On another occasion she was serving in her home again, and this time the text says simply, “Martha served,” with no mention of her being distracted (John 12:2). She had learned to serve from a place of rest in the Lord.

The adjustment is simple: before hosting, spend five quiet minutes in prayer; serve one fewer dish and talk ten minutes longer; trade “perfect” for “present.” If you find that hosting regularly leaves you drained and resentful, it may be time to scale back, find people to share the load, or take a break for a while. Love isn’t burning until there’s nothing left; it flows unceasingly from the Lord.
lessons.light: Being “distracted” in service is often a warning sign of the self-centered life: I want to prove myself, I want to be seen. Selfless service centers on the Lord and values people—people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than the menu. God first, then people, then tasks: when the order is right, even the kitchen grows quiet.
think: What was the main point of Jesus’ words to Martha?
In hosting or serving, which “many things” most often make me anxious and troubled?
Next time I host, what unnecessary task will I cut so I have more time for people?
lessons.speak: Lord, I am often like Martha, anxious and troubled about many things, even complaining about others and about you. Thank you for gently calling my name. Help me sit at your feet first and then rise to serve. When I host, let me value people over performance. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, talk with your family or roommates about the last time you hosted: Where did it get too hectic? How could you simplify and share the work next time? Write down one concrete adjustment.
lessons.quick: First sit at the Lord’s feet, then step into the kitchen.
text: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.title: When a Door Becomes a Home
lessons.hear:
When Paul and his companions arrived in Philippi, they met Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, by the riverside. The Lord opened her heart, and she and her household came to faith. The first thing she did was open her home: “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay” (Acts 16:15). Later, after Paul and Silas had been beaten, jailed, and released, the first place they went was Lydia’s house: “They went out of the prison and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them” (Acts 16:40). One open door became the starting point of the city’s first house church.

This week we have seen that hospitality is loving strangers—it doesn’t have to be perfect, only sincere. We have learned to welcome one another according to our gifts, and we have learned from Martha to be with the Lord first. For truth to become a way of life, it needs repetition. Perhaps you hosted someone once this week, and it was both sweet and tiring. Thank the Lord, and do it again. The second time is always a bit easier than the first, and by the tenth time it may have become part of your household’s culture.

The blessing of hospitality also multiplies. People who have been welcomed often understand best how to welcome others. The young woman who once ate instant noodles in that tiny studio later began treating her dorm-mates to late-night snacks. You can invite a companion to host with you—one in charge of inviting, the other of preparing. You can also let your children help set the table and greet the guests, so they learn from a young age that our door opens for others.

Paul said, “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God” (Romans 15:7). Every act of hospitality is a reenactment of the gospel: as Christ saved a place for us, we save a place for others. As door after door opens like this, God’s family is built up in the city.
lessons.light: One person’s hospitality is a dot; two or three families hosting together form a line; a whole group welcoming people consistently becomes a network. This is the most natural way to build God’s system. The spiritual companions of 235 often begin around a dinner table.
think: What was Lydia’s first action after coming to faith, and what came of it?
At what moment in this week’s hospitality did I experience God’s presence?
Which companion or family member will I invite to host with me next time?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for building your church in Philippi through Lydia’s home. Use my home too, big or small, as a place where people experience your welcome. Give me companions to host with, and let the next generation learn from our home how to open the door for others. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, invite a brother or sister or a family member to settle on who you’ll welcome together next time and when. Also share this week’s hospitality experience with your small group in three sentences.
lessons.quick: One open door can become the beginning of God’s household.
text: On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.
A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us. The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.
When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” So she persuaded us.

weeks.keyText: Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.

weeks.title: The Gospel at the Table
weeks.theme: Jesus often changed lives over a meal; a single dinner can become a doorway to grace.
group: Why was Jesus eating with sinners so offensive to people in his day?
Am I used to eating only with “our own people”? What am I afraid of?
Which friend who doesn’t yet know the Lord would you like to share a meal with this week? How can the group pray for them?
weeks.sunday: At your family table or small group meal, “add one more chair” and invite a friend who doesn’t yet know the Lord, or someone who is rarely invited anywhere. Pray for them before the meal. At the table, ask about their life and their story rather than rushing to make a point; if they’re comfortable with it, say a short grace before eating. Afterward, give thanks for this table and write down one thing you can keep caring about in their life.

lessons.title: He Eats with Sinners
lessons.hear:
In Jesus’ day, whom you ate with announced whom you accepted. So when the Pharisees saw tax collectors and sinners crowding around Jesus, they couldn’t help muttering, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). They meant it as an accusation, but without realizing it they spoke one of the most beautiful sentences in all the Gospels.

Jesus didn’t defend himself. He told a story. A shepherd has a hundred sheep; when he loses one, he leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the lost one “until he found it” (Luke 15:4). When he finds it, “he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing” (Luke 15:5), and when he gets home he calls his friends and neighbors to celebrate with him. What Jesus was doing at the dinner table was exactly what the Father does in heaven: seeking the lost, then throwing a feast to celebrate.

The table is a remarkable place. Around a conference table, people wear masks; around a dinner table, they lower their guard. Peeling shrimp together, passing dishes, refilling rice bowls—the distance closes. Once people are full, they’re ready to speak honestly. Jesus understood this. Again and again in the Gospels he changed people at the table: in Levi’s house, in Zacchaeus’s house, in a Pharisee’s house, and in the little home at Emmaus. The risen Lord “took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them,” and the disciples’ eyes were opened (see Luke 24:30-31).

Today Jesus still invites people in the same way: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). Every one of us is a sinner whom he first invited to his table. Those who have been invited will want to pull out a chair and invite someone else to sit down.
lessons.light: The Pharisees’ self-centeredness lay in guarding the purity of “our table” to prove they were better than others. Jesus’ selflessness was to give up his own reputation and sit down among sinners. When our focus is on Jesus, we are no longer afraid of being misunderstood, and our tables can change from “an insiders’ circle” into “a doorway to grace.”
think: Which phrase in the Pharisees’ complaint is actually the gospel?
Who usually sits at my table? Who is missing?
Which picture of Jesus at the table most inspires me to invite someone?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for welcoming me, a sinner, and sharing your table with me. I once thought your table was only for good people, but in truth your grace pulled me up to it. Make my table as open as yours, so that the lost can be found here. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, have lunch with a coworker or classmate—especially someone few people invite. Ask more about their story and say less about yourself.
lessons.quick: He welcomes sinners and eats with them—and I am one who was invited to the table.
text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were coming close to him to hear him.
The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.”
He told them this parable:
“Which of you men, if you had one hundred sheep and lost one of them, wouldn’t leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost, until he found it?
When he has found it, he carries it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!’
I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.

lessons.title: Afraid of a Dirty Table
lessons.hear:
After coming to faith, one brother was on fire for the Lord and started turning down every company dinner. “I don’t want anything to do with the talk and the drinking at those events anymore,” he said. A year later, he found himself increasingly isolated at the office; behind his back, coworkers said he’d “gotten religion and become stuck-up.” Once, something serious happened in a colleague’s family. Everyone knew about it except him—because he had long since stopped sitting at those tables.

Many of us carry an old mindset: spiritual people should keep their distance from “unspiritual” people, or they’ll be corrupted. That’s half right. We do need boundaries, and we shouldn’t join in anything that violates our conscience. But the other half is wrong: Jesus never kept himself holy by staying away from sinners.

Levi was a tax collector—in the eyes of his countrymen, a greedy traitor. Yet Jesus said to him, “Follow me.” Soon after, Levi threw a dinner at his house and invited many tax collectors and sinners, and Jesus sat right among them. The religious leaders demanded, “Why is it that he eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus replied, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2:16-17). A doctor doesn’t avoid the sick for fear of catching something; he comes near with the power to heal.

God’s perspective is that holiness is not isolation; it is walking in carrying the light. Jesus’ holiness is contagious. Sinners don’t stain him—he brings sinners into the light.

That brother later changed his approach. He went back to the company dinners, but he drank tea instead of alcohol, didn’t join in the dirty jokes, and didn’t preach at the table. He simply listened carefully as his coworkers talked about their kids, their mortgages, and their aging parents. Six months later, the first person to text him late at night asking for prayer was the very coworker who had called him stuck-up. “It turns out what I’d been missing wasn’t the socializing,” he said. “It was their lives.”

Keep your boundaries clear and your heart open. That’s how to be a doctor at the world’s tables rather than a deserter.
lessons.light: Keeping clean by staying away from sinners can sometimes be self-centered—it’s about protecting my image. Jesus’ holiness is selfless; he was willing to be misunderstood in order to come near those in need. To “let Jesus reign” means letting him decide which table I sit at. With him present, my boundaries stay clear and my heart stays soft.
think: When Jesus answered his critics with the image of a physician, what was his point?
Have I ever used “staying holy” as an excuse to avoid people who needed me?
At which of the world’s tables can I keep clear boundaries and still keep my heart open?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the Great Physician, and you never stayed away from sinners for fear of being misunderstood. Forgive me for so often avoiding people in need to protect my image. Help me keep my boundaries at the world’s tables while keeping my heart open, coming near my coworkers and friends with your light and gentleness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: The next time coworkers or classmates invite you to a meal, if the setting is appropriate, say yes. Decide your boundaries ahead of time, and at the table focus on listening to one person and remember one thing they mention.
lessons.quick: Holiness isn’t isolation—it’s carrying the light in.
text: He went out again by the seaside. All the multitude came to him, and he taught them.
As he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax office. He said to him, “Follow me.” And he arose and followed him.
He was reclining at the table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners sat down with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many, and they followed him.
The scribes and the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with the sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why is it that he eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners?”
When Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

lessons.title: Today I’m Coming to Your House
lessons.hear:
Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector in Jericho—wealthy but friendless. He wanted to see Jesus, so he had to climb a sycamore tree. When Jesus reached the tree, he looked up and called him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). The whole town grumbled, but Zacchaeus “received him joyfully” (Luke 19:6). At that dinner, no one records Jesus giving a grand speech. We only hear Zacchaeus stand up on his own and say he will give half his possessions to the poor and pay back four times anyone he has cheated. Before the meal was even over, salvation had come to that house.

This gives us a very practical picture of gospel friendship.

1. Start by calling them by name. Jesus knew Zacchaeus and saw the longing in his heart. Gospel friendship begins with genuinely getting to know someone, not with a script. 2. Step into their life. Share meals, grab coffee, help them move, bring a small gift on their child’s birthday. Friendship has value in itself; it is not a technique for evangelism. 3. Let the gospel flow naturally. When they ask, “How did you get through that?” share honestly what God has done in your life, and if they’re open, pray a short prayer for them.

The app has a Five Names feature, where you can write down five friends who don’t yet know the Lord and pray for them every day. Today, choose one of those five and invite them for a meal. There’s no need to rush to invite them to church or to present the whole gospel over dinner. Just be fully present, listen sincerely, and watch for the doors the Holy Spirit opens.

Use wisdom, too. If the person is of the opposite sex, choose a public place or invite one or two more friends. And don’t agree to lend money or make promises beyond your means just because you want to share the gospel. Jesus said, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). He is the one who seeks, and he is the one who saves; we simply follow him gladly and take a seat at that table.
lessons.light: Treating friends as “evangelism results” is self-centered—it’s about my achievements. Selfless gospel friendship loves the other person as someone God loves, and whether or not they believe doesn’t change the friendship. Salvation is God’s work. Our proper place is to walk alongside, to pray, and to bear witness, and to let Jesus receive all the glory.
think: How did Jesus treat Zacchaeus, and how did Zacchaeus respond?
Do I genuinely like my friends who don’t yet believe, or do I secretly treat them as a project?
Which of my Five Names could I invite for a meal this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you called Zacchaeus by name in the crowd, and you have called my name too. Help me truly love my friends and never treat them as numbers. At the table, help me listen closely and, at the right time, bear witness to your grace. Salvation is your work—please open their hearts yourself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Open the app’s Five Names, choose one friend, and text them today to set up a meal or coffee this week. Once it’s arranged, pray for that time together.
lessons.quick: Call them by name, step into their life, and let the gospel flow naturally.
text: He entered and was passing through Jericho.
There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short.
He ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way.
When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

lessons.title: Peter Left the Table
lessons.hear:
Peter was the first apostle to eat in the home of a Gentile, Cornelius, and he saw with his own eyes the Holy Spirit fall on Gentiles. If anyone understood that God doesn’t show favoritism, it should have been Peter. Yet in Antioch, “he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision” (Galatians 2:12). Worse, the other Jewish believers joined him in his hypocrisy, “so that even Barnabas was carried away” (Galatians 2:13).

When one person leaves the table, they take more than a chair. They send a message: “You aren’t good enough to eat with us.” We can imagine how those Gentile believers felt that day.

We can do the same thing. At church we’re having a great conversation with a newcomer, then a familiar core leader walks by and we leave the newcomer standing alone. At a class reunion we’re sitting with an old classmate who hasn’t done well in life, then the successful table waves us over and we find an excuse to switch seats. In a group chat we start to speak up for someone who’s being shut out, then sense which way the wind is blowing and fall silent. Peter’s problem wasn’t that he didn’t know the truth; it was that he feared people. Proverbs had long since warned, “The fear of man proves to be a snare” (Proverbs 29:25).
