Paul confronted Peter to his face because his conduct wasn’t “according to the truth of the Good News” (Galatians 2:14). Being rebuked publicly must have been painful, but Peter didn’t abandon his faith or break with Paul. Later, at the council in Jerusalem, he spoke up clearly for the Gentiles: we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are (see Acts 15:11). Late in life, he even called Paul “our beloved brother” in one of his letters (see 2 Peter 3:15).

Adjustment begins with admission: At which table did I walk away because I feared people? Then go back to that table and sit down again.
lessons.light: The root of fearing people is caring more about human approval than about God’s glory—that is the self-centered life. When Peter shrank back before people, he left his proper place in the gospel. The humble accept correction and return to their proper place. Pride provokes pride, and humility inspires humility; the later harmony between Peter and Paul was the fruit of humility.
think: Why did Peter leave the Gentiles’ table, and what effect did it have?
When have I, out of fear of people, left someone out in the cold?
How can I “go back to that table” and show that person acceptance?
lessons.speak: Lord, like Peter I have sometimes left a table I shouldn’t have left because I feared people, and made someone feel they weren’t good enough. Forgive me for caring about people’s opinions more than your heart. Give me courage to go back to that table, and humility to receive the reminders of my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone you once left out because you worried what others would think. Today, reach out with a message or a greeting in person and invite them to sit down and talk. If you embarrassed them, simply apologize.
lessons.quick: Fear of people makes us leave the table; the gospel brings us back.
text: But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.
And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.

But when I saw that they didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News, I said to Peter before them all, “If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?

lessons.title: Breaking Bread at Home
lessons.hear:
Much of the early church’s growth happened around the dinner table. Luke describes it this way: “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:46-47). No impressive buildings, no carefully designed programs—just ordinary dinner tables and a group of joyful, sincere people.

This week we’ve seen Jesus eating with sinners. We’ve learned that holiness isn’t isolation, practiced gospel friendship by inviting a friend to a meal, and faced our own weakness in leaving the table out of fear of people. For truth to take root, it needs repetition; for the gospel to spread, it needs multiplication.

Repetition means making the table a rhythm of life rather than a one-time event. Maybe it’s a monthly “one more chair” family dinner. Maybe it’s a regular weekly lunch with a coworker. Maybe it’s a simple supper before small group. It doesn’t have to be a success every time; what matters is consistency.

Multiplication means turning one table into many. Bring a companion along when you host, so they can see it isn’t that hard. Encourage every member of your small group to invite one person from their Five Names for a meal, then share and pray for each other at the next meeting. Let your children help set the table and greet the guests, and without even realizing it they’ll learn that our family’s table is prepared for others.

Paul said, “Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). A meal can simply fill our stomachs, or it can become a doorway to grace. When many Christians open their tables at the same time, little paths leading to Jesus will appear all over the city.
lessons.light: “Gladness and singleness of heart” is the flavor of a selfless table: no performance, no calculation, only joy and sincerity. Moving from one table to many tables is moving from personal life to shared ministry—life first, then relationships, then ministry. God’s system is built right there among the everyday dishes.
think: What qualities of the early church’s table does Acts 2:46-47 describe?
Was there a moment of “gladness and singleness of heart” at my table this week?
Whom will I invite to help make the table a regular rhythm?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for leading the early church to break bread at home and love one another with gladness and singleness of heart. Make my table a doorway to grace as well. With my companions and my small group, help us open more and more tables, so people may come to know your love as they eat and drink together. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, agree with your family or small group on a regular “one more chair” mealtime (for example, once a month). Put it on the calendar, and invite a companion to pray and prepare with you.
lessons.quick: Ordinary dinner tables can become little paths to Jesus.
text: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

weeks.keyText: The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.”

weeks.title: Caring for the Poor and Overlooked
weeks.theme: To see the overlooked is to see Christ; refusing to judge by appearances is a mark of the gospel.
group: In Matthew 25:31-40, why does the King say that what was done for the least was done for him?
In what settings am I most likely to treat people by appearances? Whom do I often overlook?
What concrete thing could our small group do together this week for a group of overlooked people?
weeks.sunday: With your family or small group, work through your church or a trustworthy social service agency to visit an older person who lives alone, or prepare a snack and a handwritten card for migrant workers. Pray together before you go, asking the Lord to help you see the other person’s needs rather than only your own good deed. When you get home, give thanks for the encounter and write down one thing you can keep caring about.

lessons.title: The Least of These Is He
lessons.hear:
Jesus painted a picture of the end of history: the Son of Man seated on his glorious throne, with all the nations gathered before him. The King says to those on his right, “for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat. I was thirsty and you gave me drink. I was a stranger and you took me in” (Matthew 25:35). The righteous are astonished: Lord, when did we ever do that for you? The King answers, “Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

The most startling thing about this passage is that Jesus ties himself to the most unnoticed people. The hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, those without enough clothes, the sick, the imprisoned—people society so often ignores—Jesus says, “That’s me.” It turns out he is often not under the spotlight but waiting for us in the corners of the city.

Notice that this is not a checklist for earning heaven by good deeds. The people on the right didn’t even realize they had done anything remarkable. Their good works weren’t a way of earning a reward; they were the natural overflow of lives changed by God’s love. We are saved entirely by the grace of Christ, but people who have truly been touched by grace begin to see differently. They start noticing the overlooked.

This has always been God’s heart. Proverbs says, “He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD; he will reward him” (Proverbs 19:17). God puts himself in the position of the poor person’s debtor, as if to say: whatever you do for them, I write it down on my account.

Today, “the least of these” in our cities might be the elderly patient in a hospital corridor whom no one visits, the migrant worker eating a boxed lunch beside a construction site, the grandmother still collecting cardboard after the night market closes, or the person in the group chat whose messages never get a reply. Lord, open our eyes to see you in them.
lessons.light: The self-centered size people up by their “value”: Are they useful to me? Do they make me look good? The selfless see people from God’s point of view: every person is created in the image of God, and Jesus even identifies with the least. Change your viewpoint and you change your mindset—we are not handing out charity; we are serving the Lord.
think: What overlooked needs are listed in Matthew 25:35-36?
When was the last time I truly “saw” someone who is usually overlooked?
Along my everyday routes this week, who might be “the least of these”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you identify with the least and wait for me in the overlooked. Forgive me for so often noticing only the people who are useful to me and looking right past those in the corners. Open my eyes to see you in the hungry, the lonely, and the stranger, and help me serve you with my actions. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, along your daily route, sincerely thank someone who is often overlooked—a cleaner, an elderly woman collecting recyclables, or a delivery driver—or hand them a bottle of water and tell them you appreciate their hard work.
lessons.quick: To see the overlooked is to see Christ.
text: “But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory.
Before him all the nations will be gathered, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.
He will set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.
Then the King will tell those on his right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world;
for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat. I was thirsty and you gave me drink. I was a stranger and you took me in.
I was naked and you clothed me. I was sick and you visited me. I was in prison and you came to me.’
“Then the righteous will answer him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you a drink?
When did we see you as a stranger and take you in, or naked and clothe you?
When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’
“The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’

lessons.title: “Sit Here in a Good Place”
lessons.hear:
One Sunday, two newcomers visited a church at the same time. One was a business owner who drove up in a luxury car; the welcome team member warmly led him to the front row and introduced him to the pastor. The other was a migrant worker from a nearby factory who didn’t speak the language well. He sat down by himself in the back row and slipped out quietly as soon as the service ended. No one asked his name. Later, as that team member prayed, the Holy Spirit shone a light on his heart: “I didn’t mean to, but my hands and my smile were more honest than my faith.”

James puts it bluntly. A man with a gold ring and fine clothing comes in, and you say, “Sit here in a good place”; to the poor man in filthy clothes you say, “Stand there.” Then he asks, “haven’t you shown partiality among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?” (James 2:4).

Our hearts hold a stubborn old mindset: people come in ranks, and the ones worth knowing are the ones who can help me. It shows up especially in social settings. At reunions we go first to the classmates who have done well; at community events we greet the prominent residents first; even at church we unconsciously arrange the seating this way.

God’s perspective, however, is this: “Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith” (James 2:5)? In God’s kingdom the seating chart is turned upside down; the person we put in the back row may be in the front row in God’s eyes. Showing favoritism isn’t just bad manners. James says, “if you show partiality, you commit sin” (James 2:9), because it violates the royal law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

That team member later learned a few simple greetings in Indonesian and Vietnamese, set up a “newcomer seat” at the church entrance, and asked brothers and sisters of different nationalities to take turns sitting with visitors. Six months later, the church had a small fellowship for migrant workers. Change didn’t start with a grand plan; it started with a single chair.
lessons.light: Treating people by appearances is the self-centered life doing its math: whom should I befriend for my own benefit? Selfless love doesn’t calculate, because we ourselves were accepted by God when we had nothing. Pride makes us look up to some and step on others; humility brings us back to our proper place. At the foot of the cross, everyone needs grace equally and is loved equally.
think: In James 2:1-9, why is showing partiality a violation of “love your neighbor as yourself”?
In my social circles, whom do I usually seat in the “good place,” and whom in the “back row”?
At the next gathering or event, which back-row person could I reach out to and sit with?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you show no partiality, and you accepted me when I had nothing. Forgive me for so often treating people according to appearance, status, or ability, and sending some to the back row of my heart. Renew my vision so I see every person through your love, and help me save a good seat for those who are overlooked. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: At a gathering or community event this week, go up to someone sitting alone who seems out of place. Sit next to them, ask their name, and chat with them for a few minutes.
lessons.quick: In God’s kingdom, those in the back row may be seated in the front.
text: My brothers, don’t hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality.
For if a man with a gold ring, in fine clothing, comes into your synagogue, and a poor man in filthy clothing also comes in,
and you pay special attention to him who wears the fine clothing and say, “Sit here in a good place;” and you tell the poor man, “Stand there,” or “Sit by my footstool”
haven’t you shown partiality among yourselves, and become judges with evil thoughts?
Listen, my beloved brothers. Didn’t God choose those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom which he promised to those who love him?
But you have dishonored the poor man. Don’t the rich oppress you and personally drag you before the courts?
Don’t they blaspheme the honorable name by which you are called?
However, if you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well.
But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.

lessons.title: Invite Those Who Can’t Repay
lessons.hear:
Once, while Jesus was eating at the home of a leading Pharisee, he noticed the guests jockeying for the places of honor, and that the host had invited only prominent friends. Jesus said to his host, “But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind; and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you” (Luke 14:13-14).

These words challenge the whole logic of our social lives. When we invite people for a meal, we usually do some “you scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours” calculating: I treat you, and next time you treat me; I help you, and later you’ll remember me. Jesus asks us to do something that “doesn’t pay”: love those who can’t pay us back. Precisely because they can’t repay, that love is pure—and most like God’s love.

You can begin today, and you don’t have to do it alone.

1. A personal step: visit an older person who lives alone, share lunch with them, and listen to stories from their younger days; or bring a snack to migrant workers and use a translation app to say, “Thank you for all your hard work here.” 2. Walk with your church: join your church’s care visits, food bank, or tutoring ministry, and let experienced team members guide you. 3. Partner with your community: many social service agencies, neighborhood offices, and senior centers need volunteers. Christians quietly serving there is a witness in itself.

Helping people takes wisdom, too. Don’t casually hand large sums of cash to people you don’t know. Instead, you can buy them a meal, accompany them to the appropriate agency for help, or assist through your church’s care ministry and trustworthy organizations. When visiting, go in pairs. Respect people’s wishes and dignity; don’t take photos to show off, and don’t treat people as subjects for your camera.

When we serve those on the margins, we often think we are the ones giving. Later we discover that we ourselves have been deeply blessed by their simple gratitude and resilient lives. Jesus said, “For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14:14). God keeps the accounts himself, and he never shortchanges anyone.
lessons.light: “You scratch my back” socializing is the head doing its calculations; “inviting those who can’t repay” is the love of the heart. Living from the head breeds worry—fear of losing out. Living from the heart brings joy—experiencing God’s abundance in giving. Denying ourselves is for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves; that is the logic of the cross.
think: Why did Jesus specifically tell his host to invite those who “don’t have the resources to repay”?
How many of my relationships come with an expectation of something in return?
What concrete thing can I do this week for someone who can’t repay me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, when you gave your life for me, I had nothing to repay you with. Take away the tit-for-tat calculating in my heart and make me glad to love those who can’t pay me back. Give me wisdom to work alongside my church and trustworthy organizations, serving in ways that are respectful and safe. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact your church’s care ministry or a local senior center and ask about a visitation or volunteer opportunity you can join—or invite a companion to visit an older person who lives alone with you this week.
lessons.quick: Loving those who can’t repay is most like God’s love.
text: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you make a dinner or a supper, don’t call your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, or perhaps they might also return the favor, and pay you back.
But when you make a feast, ask the poor, the maimed, the lame, or the blind;
and you will be blessed, because they don’t have the resources to repay you. For you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.”

lessons.title: Those Who Told Him to Be Quiet
lessons.hear:
Outside Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus sat by the road. When he heard that Jesus was passing by, he began to shout, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:47). The result: “Many rebuked him, that he should be quiet” (Mark 10:48). These people probably weren’t bad. Perhaps they were excitedly following Jesus and felt this beggar was too loud, too unsightly, an interruption to an important journey.

This scene is worth examining ourselves by. We are often that crowd. In the community group chat, someone keeps complaining about how hard life is, and everyone dismisses it as negativity and mutes them. At church, a brother is emotionally unstable and says awkward things, so we steer clear of him. At work, a foreign coworker has a question, and we decide the language barrier makes him too much trouble. We don’t drive them away; we just make sure they “should be quiet.”

Self-centered social life always wants to keep the atmosphere comfortable and respectable, and anyone who disrupts it gets pushed to the edges.

But “Jesus stood still.” He stopped the whole procession and said, “Call him.” Here comes the most beautiful turn: the same crowd that had just rebuked Bartimaeus turned and said to him, “Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!” (Mark 10:49). They went from being the ones who blocked him to being the ones who passed on the call. What changed them was the moment they saw Jesus stop.

Adjustment starts here too. When we see whom Jesus stops for, we learn to stop for them as well. Ask yourself today: Whom have I put on “mute” in my heart? Then ask the Lord for courage to say to that person, “Cheer up! Get up.” And remember that if their struggles involve long-term mental or physical difficulties, encouraging them to seek counseling or medical help is also part of loving them.
lessons.light: The crowd’s self-centeredness put their own convenience ahead of another person’s cry for help. Jesus’ selflessness stopped an entire journey for one beggar. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than plans. When our focus returns to Jesus, we stop being those who block people and become those who bring people to the Lord.
think: How did the crowd’s attitude toward Bartimaeus change from beginning to end?
Whom have I put on “mute” in my heart, not wanting to hear them anymore?
How can I “stand still” for that person and really listen to them once?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you stopped in your tracks for a blind beggar. Forgive me for so often finding others too noisy or too much trouble and making them be quiet around me. Help me stop for people as you do, and turn me from someone who blocks people into someone who brings them to you and says, “Cheer up! Get up.” In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of someone in a group chat or in daily life whom you’ve deliberately ignored because they seem like too much trouble. Reach out with a message or a call, and really listen to them for ten minutes without rushing to give advice.
lessons.quick: Whomever Jesus stops for, I will stop for too.
text: They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!”
Many rebuked him, that he should be quiet, but he cried out much more, “You son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stood still and said, “Call him.” They called the blind man, saying to him, “Cheer up! Get up. He is calling you!”
He, casting away his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.
Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabboni, that I may see again.”
Jesus said to him, “Go your way. Your faith has made you well.” Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the way.

lessons.title: Caring Together as a Church
lessons.hear:
The early church grew quickly, and problems came with it: “a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service” (Acts 6:1). These widows were mostly Jews who had returned to Jerusalem from elsewhere, with a language and culture different from the locals’—in today’s terms, the most vulnerable members of an immigrant community.

The apostles didn’t deny the problem or tell people to “just be a little more patient.” They gathered all the disciples and had them choose “seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom” (Acts 6:3) to take charge of it. Interestingly, all seven have Greek names. Many interpreters believe the church likely chose people culturally close to the neglected group to serve them. The result: “The word of God increased” (Acts 6:7). Caring for those on the margins didn’t slow the gospel down—it made it flourish all the more.

This week we’ve seen that the least of these is Christ, learned not to treat people by appearances, practiced inviting those who can’t repay, and examined whether we have told others to be quiet. For truth to take root, it needs repetition; for love to last, it needs a team.

One person’s enthusiasm burns out easily, but a group of people of one heart can go the distance. You can bring what you’ve received this week to your small group and discuss a group you could adopt together: older people living alone nearby, migrant workers, new immigrant families, children with no one to look after them after school. You can also find out what care ministries your church already has, sign up to join, or refer needs around you to the team members responsible. When it comes to social issues, Christians may hold different political views, but seeing people and serving them is our shared calling.

Paul said the church leaders asked only one thing of him: “They only asked us to remember the poor” (Galatians 2:10). May our church become the place in the city that best knows how to remember the poor, and may this remembering be passed on to the next generation.
lessons.light: The way Acts 6 handled the problem shows the last layer of the five-fold change: moving from personal life and relationships into organized ministry. We build God’s system not by relying on one or two heroes, but by letting every member serve in the right place. People filled with the Holy Spirit, working together, make the overlooked seen.
think: How did the apostles handle the neglect of the widows, and what was the result?
Do I tend to do good on my own without inviting others to join me?
Whom can I invite, or which ministry can I join, to care for people on the margins this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that the early church did not ignore its marginalized widows. Help our church and small group see the overlooked with one heart, and each serve in our own part. Raise me and my companions up to remember the poor together, and to pass this love on to the next generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, share what you’ve received this week in three sentences with your small group or a companion, propose adopting one specific group or person to care for together, and set a date for your first step.
lessons.quick: One person’s zeal burns out; a group of one heart goes the distance.
text: Now in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplying, a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service.
The twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples and said, “It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables.
Therefore, select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word.”
These words pleased the whole multitude. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch,
whom they set before the apostles. When they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.
The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.

weeks.keyText: He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD; he will reward him.

weeks.title: Seek the Peace of the City
weeks.theme: We are citizens of heaven and good neighbors on earth—praying for our city and working for our community.
group: Jeremiah told the exiles to “seek the peace of the city.” What does that say to us today?
Toward my own community, do I tend more to complain and stay detached, or to pray and get involved?
What concrete act of service could we do together for our community this week?
weeks.sunday: Take a slow walk around your neighborhood with your family or a companion. As you pass the school, the market, the clinic, the park, and the police station, quietly pray a sentence for the people there. If your community has a cleanup, a market day, or a volunteer event, sign up to take part once. Before you set out, ask the Lord to give you eyes to see your community; when you get home, give thanks together for your city and write down one need you can keep praying for.

lessons.title: Building Houses in Babylon
lessons.hear:
When the people of Judah were carried off to Babylon, their hearts must have been full of humiliation and homesickness. Some prophets told them they would soon be going home, so there was no need to invest much where they were. But Jeremiah wrote a surprising letter: “Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit” (Jeremiah 29:5). More than that: “Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace” (Jeremiah 29:7).

That is an astonishing command. Babylon was the city that had torn down their temple, yet God told them to pray and work for its good. The “peace” here means more than the absence of war. It means the wholeness, flourishing, and goodness of the entire city—safe streets, harmonious families, fair business, the elderly and weak cared for.

Our situation is a little like that of the exiles. Paul says, “For our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20); this world is not our final home. But being citizens of heaven doesn’t mean being passersby on earth who don’t care about anything. Precisely because we belong to heaven, we can see with heaven’s eyes and be the best neighbors on earth. The Lord’s Prayer says, “Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). That “earth” includes the street we live on, our apartment building, our neighborhood.

For many overseas Chinese, new immigrants, and young people who have moved to a big city for work, “the city where you live” may not be your hometown. God’s word comforts us: you are not here by accident. God “caused” you to be carried to this city, and he wants to bless the city through you. Don’t just wait to leave. Put down roots here, build, plant—and pray here too.

Later in his letter, Jeremiah adds a promise: God’s thoughts toward his people are “thoughts of peace, and not of evil” (Jeremiah 29:11). God has thoughts of peace toward our cities as well, and we are the messengers of peace he sends.
lessons.light: Treating the city only as a place to sleep and earn money is self-centered—the city exists to serve me. The selfless ask instead: While I’m here, how can I make this city better? This is what it means to build God’s system: the coming of God’s kingdom doesn’t happen only in church, but also in the everyday life of our neighborhoods, streets, and apartment buildings.
think: In Jeremiah 29:4-7, what does God tell the exiles to do?
Toward my city or neighborhood, do I have a “just passing through” mindset or a “putting down roots” mindset?
Which place or group of people in this city most needs peace?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for placing me in this city—it is no accident. Forgive me for so often treating it like a traveler’s inn, complaining instead of praying. Help me seek the peace of this city, praying for its families, schools, streets, and every person here. Help me put down roots and be your messenger of peace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: As you commute or go out today, silently pray a sentence for the people in every place you pass—school, hospital, market, office building: “May peace come to this place.”
lessons.quick: Seek the peace of the city, because God has placed me here.
text: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:
“Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.
Take wives and father sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters. Multiply there, and don’t be diminished.
Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”

lessons.title: Pilgrims Can Be Good Neighbors
lessons.hear:
A new residential community held its first owners’ meeting, and it quickly turned into a shouting match. Parking spaces, management fees, repairs to common areas—every item had someone pounding the table. One sister had planned to sit quietly in the back, thinking, “This is all worldly stuff. It has nothing to do with my faith. I’ll just see how it turns out after they finish arguing.” After the meeting, she watched one attacking message after another pour into the community group chat, and suddenly it struck her: Did God put me here just to stand by and watch?

We often carry two old mindsets. One is withdrawal: this world is passing away, so community and public affairs have nothing to do with spiritual life. The other is cynicism: whenever the homeowners’ board, local officials, or the government comes up, all we do is complain and mock. Both place us outside the city.

Peter wrote to Christians who were misunderstood and pushed to the margins. He called them “foreigners and pilgrims,” yet he told them to keep “having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:11-12). Being pilgrims isn’t a reason to withdraw; it is a call to take part differently—not grabbing for power, not hurling insults, but answering with good works.

Peter sums it up in one line: “Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17). “Honor all men” includes neighbors who disagree with you, residents on the other side of an issue, and people you didn’t vote for. That doesn’t mean we can’t express our views; it means we express them without losing respect. Nor does it mean Christians must pick a side; it means being a child of peace in whatever camp we find ourselves.

That sister later volunteered for the board’s environment committee. In the group chat, she gently summarized everyone’s opinions, and she suggested holding a residents’ social in the courtyard. A year later, a resident remarked, “Our community seems a lot less contentious now.” She smiled: “I just didn’t want to be a spectator in the back row anymore.”
lessons.light: Withdrawal and cynicism are both self-centered: one dodges responsibility, the other wants everyone to do things my way. Selfless citizens live “as bondservants of God”—taking part through good works, speaking with respect, and letting Jesus reign rather than letting our positions reign. Humility inspires humility; one gentle person can cool down an entire group chat.
think: According to 1 Peter 2:11-17, how should “foreigners and pilgrims” live in society?
Toward my community or public affairs, do I lean toward withdrawal or cynicism?
In community group chats or meetings, how can I take part with good works and respect?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I am a citizen of heaven and also part of this community. Forgive me for sometimes standing by coldly and sometimes complaining bitterly. Help me live with good behavior and honor all people, being a child of peace wherever opinions differ, so that people may see your glory through good works. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in your community group chat or in conversation with residents, publicly thank someone who serves quietly—the building manager, a cleaner, a board member, or a local official.
lessons.quick: Pilgrims don’t withdraw; they take part in the city through good works.
text: Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul,
having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.
Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme,
or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well.
For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.
Live as free people, yet not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.
Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.

lessons.title: Prayers for All People
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote young Timothy a guide for pastoring, and the first item wasn’t organizational structure but prayer: “I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men, for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence” (1 Timothy 2:1-2).

The king at that time was the Roman emperor, who did not support Christians and might even persecute them. Yet Paul told the church to pray for him. Praying for those in authority doesn’t mean endorsing everything they do. It means acknowledging that God is Lord of history and placing our cities and nations in his hands. Prayer is the most powerful—and most often overlooked—contribution Christians make to their cities.

Today you can pray for your city like this.

1. For those in authority: neighborhood leaders, the homeowners’ board, local officials, police and firefighters, healthcare workers, teachers. Ask God to give them wisdom, justice, and health, whatever party they belong to. 2. For those in need: older people living alone, single-parent families, migrant workers, new immigrants, the unemployed, the homeless, the oppressed. Ask God to protect and provide for them and to send people to help. 3. For open doors for the gospel: because God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), ask him to raise up more ambassadors of reconciliation in this city.

After you pray, let your prayers grow feet. You could join a neighborhood cleanup, donate blood, or help with a disaster-preparedness drill. During election season, you can refuse to forward unverified information or attack people in group chats. Together with your church, you can partner with community organizations to adopt a park, a school, or a senior center and serve there consistently.

Prayer and action are like two legs; you need both. Prayer without action easily becomes empty words; action without prayer easily leads to burnout or loses its way. Put them together, and the city will gradually feel the warmth of the kingdom of heaven.
lessons.light: Praying for those in authority and for all people is returning to our proper place as human beings: acknowledging that God is the city’s true King. The proud only criticize; the humble intercede first. To let Jesus reign doesn’t depend on our holding power; it comes through prayer and service, so that God’s will is done on earth as it is in heaven.
think: Whom does 1 Timothy 2:1-4 tell us to pray for, and why?
Do I pray for those in authority more often or less often than I criticize them?
Which three kinds of people in my city can I pray for specifically today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I pray for the city where I live. Give those in authority wisdom and justice. Protect our healthcare workers, police, firefighters, and teachers. Watch over the elderly who live alone, migrant workers, and those without jobs. Make me someone who not only criticizes but gladly intercedes and serves, so that your peace comes to this city. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three prayer focuses for your city (one person in authority, one group in need, and one gospel need) and pray for them every morning. Also look up one community service opportunity you can join this month.
lessons.quick: Prayer is the best gift Christians can give their city.
text: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,
for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,
who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.

lessons.title: Jonah Outside the City
lessons.hear:
Jonah did eventually go to Nineveh and deliver God’s message. The whole city repented, and God did not bring disaster. You’d think this would be a preacher’s greatest success, yet “it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry” (Jonah 4:1). He went out and sat east of the city, made himself a shelter, and waited “until he might see what would become of the city” (Jonah 4:5)—probably still hoping fire would fall from heaven.

Jonah’s problem wasn’t that he didn’t know God was merciful. On the contrary, he knew it all too well, and that was why he was angry. He wanted God’s mercy reserved for his own people, not given to a city he despised.

We can be Jonahs sitting outside the city, too. We have nothing but criticism for the city we live in: the traffic is chaos, people are cold, the politics are rotten. Toward some group in our community—an ethnic group, people with certain views, residents of “low quality”—we secretly hope they’ll get what’s coming to them. We don’t take part and we don’t bless; we just sit under our own shelter and coldly watch to see how the city ends up.

God didn’t scold Jonah. He gently taught him through a vine. When Jonah grieved over a plant that had sprung up overnight, God asked him, “Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?” (Jonah 4:11).

The book of Jonah ends on that question and never tells us how Jonah answered. It seems the question is left for every reader. God’s concern isn’t only for us; it also includes the city and the people we can’t stand.

The first step of adjustment is to leave the shelter outside the city. Admit your indifference and bitterness, and ask God to put in your heart his own concern for this city. Then pray sincerely, just once, for the person or group you find hardest to bless. When we begin to seek the peace of the city, our own hearts find peace first.
lessons.light: Jonah’s anger is the self-centered life at its extreme: wanting God to carry out judgment according to my likes and dislikes. That is leaving our proper place and trying to take God’s place. Humility is returning to our proper place and letting God be God. Whom he loves and whom he forgives is his decision; our part is to share his heart and care for the city he cares for.
think: Why was Jonah angry that Nineveh was spared?
Is there a city or a group of people in my heart that I secretly don’t want to see do well?
How can I “leave the shelter” and pray for them or do something good for them?
lessons.speak: Lord, I am often like Jonah, sitting outside the city watching coldly, even hoping certain people will suffer a little. Forgive my bitterness and pride, and put your concern for this city inside me. Help me leave my shelter and bless and pray for the people and groups I can’t stand. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, sincerely pray for God to bless the group you find hardest to bless, or a neighbor whose views differ from yours. And make a point of not forwarding any message that mocks or attacks them.
lessons.quick: God cares for this city, so I won’t sit outside it watching coldly anymore.
text: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.

He prayed to the LORD, and said, “Please, LORD, wasn’t this what I said when I was still in my own country? Therefore I hurried to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and you relent of doing harm.
Therefore now, LORD, take, I beg you, my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
The LORD said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”
Then Jonah went out of the city and sat on the east side of the city, and there made himself a booth and sat under it in the shade, until he might see what would become of the city.
The LORD God prepared a vine and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head to deliver him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the vine.
But God prepared a worm at dawn the next day, and it chewed on the vine so that it withered.

When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he was faint and requested for himself that he might die. He said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “I am right to be angry, even to death.”
The LORD said, “You have been concerned for the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow; which came up in a night and perished in a night.

Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?”

lessons.title: Let’s Rise Up and Build
lessons.hear:
When Nehemiah heard that Jerusalem’s walls were broken down and its gates burned, he sat down and wept, fasting and praying. But he didn’t stay in his tears; he carried his prayers into action. He went back to Jerusalem and said to the people, “Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.” And the people answered, “Let’s rise up and build” (Nehemiah 2:17-18).

Nehemiah’s way of rebuilding the wall gives us a clear picture: pray first, then survey the situation, then invite everyone to work together. Later the text tells us that many made repairs, “everyone across from his own house” (Nehemiah 3:28), and so the wall was joined together. One person can’t repair an entire city, but when each person repairs their own section, the city is rebuilt.

This week we’ve learned to seek the peace of the city where we live, to be pilgrims who honor all people, to pray for all people, and to examine whether we, like Jonah, are watching coldly from outside. For truth to take root, it needs repetition; for a city to change, it needs co-workers.

You can start with “the section in front of your own house”: your own apartment building, your lane, your child’s school, the market you visit regularly. Keep praying for it, and keep doing one small good thing. Then invite companions. Your small group could adopt a community site together, partnering with the neighborhood office, a school, or a social service agency. You can also teach your children the habit of praying for the city, so that each day as they head out they speak a blessing over the people they pass.

Of course, some will sneer as Sanballat did: “What is this thing that you are doing?” Nehemiah’s answer was simple: “The God of heaven will prosper us. Therefore we, his servants, will arise and build” (Nehemiah 2:20). We don’t work for applause; we work because we trust God.

Proverbs says, “By the blessing of the upright, the city is exalted” (Proverbs 11:11). May our cities be blessed through many ordinary but upright Christians.
lessons.light: Nehemiah’s wall is a model of 235 and team ministry: first with God (prayer), then with people (invitation), then with the task (building). When the order of relationships is right, ministry has power. One section per person, all joined together—this is what God’s system looks like as it is built up in a city.
think: What key things did Nehemiah do before and during the rebuilding of the wall?
What is “the section of wall in front of my house”—which place or group?
Whom will I invite to pray for and serve our community with me?
lessons.speak: God of heaven, make me like Nehemiah—weeping and praying over the broken places of my city, and then rising up to build. Give me companions to repair the section in front of our own doors, working with our community and joined together. In the face of ridicule, help us trust in you alone. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, connect with a brother or sister or a family member and choose the section “in front of your door”—a building, a school, or a park. Agree to go on a prayer walk around it together this month and to do one specific act of service there.
lessons.quick: When each one repairs a section, the wall comes together.
text: Then I said to them, “You see the bad situation that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste, and its gates are burned with fire. Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.”

I told them about the hand of my God which was good on me, and also about the king’s words that he had spoken to me. They said, “Let’s rise up and build.” So they strengthened their hands for the good work.

But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite servant, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they ridiculed us and despised us, and said, “What is this thing that you are doing? Will you rebel against the king?”
Then I answered them, and said to them, “The God of heaven will prosper us. Therefore we, his servants, will arise and build; but you have no portion, nor right, nor memorial in Jerusalem.”

weeks.keyText: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”

weeks.title: Where Conflict Comes From
weeks.theme: Conflict is rooted in the cravings of our own hearts; deal with your own heart first, then with the issues between you.
group: James says our fights come from our own cravings. Do you agree? Share an example.
Think back to your most recent conflict. What did I really want but couldn’t get?
With whom are you experiencing friction, and which one of your own insistences do you want to lay down first this week?
weeks.sunday: Share a relaxed meal with your family or roommates. Afterward, each person shares one small thing they’ve recently “insisted on but could actually let go of,” such as how chores are divided, where to eat, or daily schedules. Pray together before you begin, asking the Lord to shine his light on your hearts. When sharing, speak only about yourself, without blaming anyone else. Finish by giving thanks for one another’s honesty, and concretely yield on one thing.

lessons.title: Wars Begin in the Heart
lessons.hear:
James asks a question that goes straight to the core: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1). We tend to locate the causes of conflict outside ourselves: the other person is too selfish, the system is unfair, resources are scarce, the timing is wrong. James turns the flashlight inward. Quarrels don’t invade from outside; they overflow from within.

The “pleasures” here aren’t necessarily evil desires. Often they’re simply “I want”: I want to be respected, to be noticed, to do it my way, to win. These longings aren’t always wrong in themselves. The problem is that when they take the throne of our hearts, we will fight to get them. James says, “You lust, and don’t have” (James 4:2). When we fight to get what we want, we often end up losing both ways: the task doesn’t get done, and the relationship breaks too.

James also points to the way out: “You don’t have, because you don’t ask” (James 4:2). Many conflicts happen because, instead of first bringing our needs to God, we rush to grab them from people. When we ask God first and find our satisfaction in him, we no longer need to snatch things from others.

Then comes a line full of hope: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). There are two roads through conflict. On the road of pride, the more we argue, the harder we become—and God himself opposes us. On the road of humility, we bow our heads first, and God’s grace comes to us all the more.

So James’s prescription isn’t to change the other person first. It is this: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:8). Before dealing with the issues between us, deal with your own heart. Before demanding that others give way, let Jesus take the throne again. When the war inside stops, the war outside has a chance for a ceasefire.
lessons.light: The root of conflict is the self-centered life—“I” sit on the throne and want everyone to do things my way. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. When we let Jesus reign, our cravings step down. Once our relationship with God is right, there is room for our relationships with people to be repaired.
think: In James 4:1-3, how is conflict related to “not having”?
In my most recent conflict, what did I want most?
What can I “ask” God for today instead of grabbing it from people?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that many of my quarrels don’t come from other people but from the cravings in my own heart. I want to win, to be respected, to have my own way. Take the throne of my heart again. Help me draw near to you first and find my satisfaction in you, and give me humility so I can receive more of your grace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, think back to your most recent friction with someone and quietly write down: What did I really want at the time? Then hand that desire over to God in a one-sentence prayer.
lessons.quick: Quarrels don’t invade from outside; they overflow from the heart.
text: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

lessons.title: Too Little Land, or Too Little Heart?
lessons.hear:
Two college friends opened a small coffee shop together. The first year was sweet. In the second year, business picked up—and the friction began: who should get a bigger share of the profits, whether to change the menu, whose relatives could drink coffee for free. Each felt shortchanged: “I’ve put in more. What gives him the right?” In the end, more than ten years of friendship and the shop came to an end together. They always thought the problem was how the profits were split, yet the more profit there was, the worse the fighting got.

Abram and Lot faced something similar. The text says, “The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together; for their possessions were so great that they couldn’t live together” (Genesis 13:6). It wasn’t poverty that made them quarrel; it was abundance. The herdsmen fought over water and pasture, and cracks began to appear in the family.

Our old mindset says conflict happens because resources are limited or the other person is unreasonable; if I just secure what I’m owed, there will be peace. But experience tells us that however many resources there are, if the heart isn’t big enough, there still won’t be room.

Abram did something surprising. He was the elder, the heir of God’s promise, and he could have chosen first. Instead he said, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me … for we are relatives. Isn’t the whole land before you?” (Genesis 13:8-9). He gave Lot the right to choose. Lot chose the plain that looked best watered and moved his tents step by step until he reached Sodom. Abram stayed in Canaan, and God immediately renewed his promise to him.

God’s perspective is that relationships matter more than things, and people matter more than tasks. Abram could give way because he believed God was his inheritance; he didn’t need to grab things to secure his future.

Of course, yielding doesn’t mean letting people walk all over you. Contracts, finances, and legal responsibilities still need to be clearly spelled out, and when necessary you can ask a trustworthy third party to help. But before you negotiate terms, ask yourself: Is the problem that there isn’t enough land, or that there isn’t enough room in my heart?
lessons.light: Abram’s yielding is the freedom of the selfless life: his focus was on God’s promise, not immediate gain. Lot’s choosing was self-centered shrewdness, yet it led him step by step toward Sodom. Denying ourselves isn’t a loss; it is entrusting our future to God. What we fight to get isn’t necessarily a blessing.
think: What caused the conflict between Abram and Lot, and how did Abram handle it?
In a current point of friction, is the problem too little land or too little heart?
In what matter can I follow Abram’s example and let the other person choose first?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you are my inheritance; I don’t need to fight to secure my future. Forgive me for so often contending with people over possessions, advantage, and saving face, and tearing relationships apart. Enlarge my heart so that, like Abram, I give way first where it is fitting. And give me wisdom to state clearly what needs to be made clear. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, on some small matter where you and a family member, coworker, or roommate disagree (such as where to eat or who does what first), take the initiative and say, “You choose first.” Then, in your heart, entrust the result to God.
lessons.quick: When the heart has room, the land has room too.
text: Lot also, who went with Abram, had flocks, herds, and tents.
The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together; for their possessions were so great that they couldn’t live together.
There was strife between the herdsmen of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s livestock. The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time.
Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.
Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.”

Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar.
So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one another.
Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom.

lessons.title: Pause Before You Speak
lessons.hear:
Conflict often escalates within seconds: one remark, one tone of voice, one message left on read, and the fire is lit. Proverbs offers a simple but powerful principle: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). With the same situation, different answers can either calm a storm or turn a spark into a blaze.

Another proverb says, “Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice” (Proverbs 13:10). Many conflicts aren’t really about differing opinions but about both sides wanting to prove “I’m right.”

When friction arises today, you can practice three steps.

1. Pause: before replying to a message or opening your mouth, stop for ten seconds, take a deep breath, and pray silently: “Lord, what do I really want right now?” That pause gives the Holy Spirit room to speak. 2. Listen: seek to understand before seeking to be understood. James reminds us, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Try restating what the other person means: “So you feel that… is that right?” 3. Soften: express your own feelings and needs in a gentle tone. Say “I feel” more often and “you always” less often. When necessary, set a time to talk again when you’re both calm, and don’t argue publicly in a group chat.

These three steps aren’t techniques; they are training so that “A gentle tongue is a tree of life” (Proverbs 15:4) becomes true of us.

A word of caution: if a conflict involves violence, threats, stalking, or bullying, don’t try to tough it out alone, and don’t stay silent “for the sake of peace.” First make sure you and your family are safe, and seek help from trusted people, the relevant authorities, or professionals—that, too, is wisdom. And if a conflict leaves you anxious and sleepless for a long time, seeking counseling is also God’s grace.
lessons.light: “Pausing” is living from the heart and relying on the Holy Spirit; “snapping back right away” is living from the head and relying on ourselves. Living from the heart brings joy; living from the head breeds worry. The issues of life flow from the heart. A gentle answer isn’t weakness—it lets Jesus reign in that moment and lets the gentleness of the Spirit flow through our tongues.
think: In Proverbs 15:1-4, what results do gentle words and harsh words each bring?
In conflict, what do I do most often—interrupt, bring up the past, or give the silent treatment?
If friction comes up today, how will I practice “Pause, Listen, Soften”?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, stop me in the moment I want to snap back. Help me pause and ask what my heart really wants. Give me the patience to be swift to hear and slow to speak, and give me a gentle tongue. And if I face danger or mistreatment, give me wisdom to seek help. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you disagree with someone, first pause and pray silently for ten seconds, then restate the other person’s point in one sentence before sharing your own view. Tonight, review how the practice went.
lessons.quick: Pause, listen well, speak gently—and anger is half gone.
text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.

lessons.title: The Surface Reason and the Real Grievance
lessons.hear:
Miriam and Aaron were Moses’s older sister and brother, and longtime partners in leading the people. One day they began criticizing Moses: “Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married” (Numbers 12:1). On the surface, the conflict was about a marriage. But then they voiced what they really felt: “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” (Numbers 12:2).

It turns out the marriage was only the surface reason. The real grievance was: Why him and not us? Many conflicts have two layers. Out loud we argue about an unfair schedule, where to have dinner, who didn’t reply to a message; deep down, what really hurts is feeling unvalued or outshone. If we deal only with the surface, as soon as one argument ends, the next one pops up.

Notice a quiet phrase in the text: “And the LORD heard it” (Numbers 12:2). Talk behind someone’s back is never really “behind” anyone’s back. And look at Moses: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth” (Numbers 12:3). He didn’t call a press conference to defend himself; he let God vindicate him.

Later Miriam was struck with leprosy, and Aaron came to his senses. He said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned” (Numbers 12:11). And Moses, the one who had been slandered, responded first by crying out for his sister: “Heal her, God, I beg you!” (Numbers 12:13). Miriam was shut outside the camp for seven days, yet the whole people waited for her and didn’t move on until she was brought back (see Numbers 12:15). God disciplined, and he also restored—and the community did not leave her behind.

Today, review yourself with two questions. First, in my latest conflict, what was the surface reason, and what was the real grievance underneath? Admit it honestly to God and, like Aaron, say, “I have done foolishly.” Second, if I’m the one being talked about, can I resist rushing to defend myself and pray for that person instead? Adjustment means bringing the real issue to God—and bringing the one who hurt me to God as well.
lessons.light: “Why him and not me?” is the voice of the self-centered life. Comparison drives us out of our proper place and makes us grasp for a position that isn’t ours. Moses’s humility is returning to our proper place: letting God be God and leaving vindication to him. Humility inspires humility—when the slandered pray for the slanderer, conflict turns from judgment to healing.
think: In Numbers 12:1-2, how did what Miriam and Aaron said differ from what they really felt?
What is the real grievance underneath my latest conflict?
For which person who has talked about me can I pray, “Heal them, God”?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often cover the comparison and resentment in my heart with surface reasons. Shine your light on my true motives, and help me, like Aaron, admit my foolishness. Give me the humility of Moses, so that when I’m misunderstood I don’t rush to defend myself but pray for those who have hurt me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the two layers of your latest conflict: “On the surface we were arguing about…” and “What I really resented was….” Bring the second sentence to God, and pray once for the other person.
lessons.quick: We argue about surface things; what hurts is “Why not me?”
text: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the Cushite woman whom he had married; for he had married a Cushite woman.
They said, “Has the LORD indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?” And the LORD heard it.
Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.
The LORD’s anger burned against them; and he departed.
The cloud departed from over the Tent; and behold, Miriam was leprous, as white as snow. Aaron looked at Miriam, and behold, she was leprous.
Aaron said to Moses, “Oh, my lord, please don’t count this sin against us, in which we have done foolishly, and in which we have sinned.
Let her not, I pray, be as one dead, of whom the flesh is half consumed when he comes out of his mother’s womb.”
Moses cried to the LORD, saying, “Heal her, God, I beg you!”

lessons.title: Don’t Take Sides—Build Together
lessons.hear:
The church in Corinth had many gifts—and many conflicts. Believers rallied around their favorite leaders: “For when one says, ‘I follow Paul,’ and another, ‘I follow Apollos,’ aren’t you fleshly?” (1 Corinthians 3:4). Paul cut to the heart of it: “For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). Today’s version sounds familiar: a “Pastor So-and-So camp” at church, a family group chat split into two sides, a colleague at work asking, “Whose side are you on?”

Paul’s prescription is striking. First he puts the people everyone looks up to back in their proper place: “Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed” (1 Corinthians 3:5). Then he turns everyone’s eyes to God: “For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9). If a field is split into two factions, no one gets a harvest; if everyone in a house tears down a different wall, no one has a home to live in.

This week we’ve seen from James that conflict springs from the cravings of the heart. From Abram we learned the freedom of saying, “You choose first.” We practiced “Pause, Listen, Soften.” And in Miriam we saw that beneath the surface reasons there often lies the grievance, “Why not me?” The way out of all of this points in one direction: when Jesus takes the throne again, we no longer need to grab for position or recruit supporters.

Repetition means that the next time someone says to you, “You be the judge—isn’t he the one in the wrong?” you pause and ask yourself: Am I expanding a faction right now, or building God’s house? You can listen to their hurt without rushing to take sides, pray with them, and encourage them to go and talk with that person directly.

Multiplication means bringing this culture into your small group, family, or team. Agree together that when there’s disagreement, you’ll bring people to the Lord rather than pull them into your own camp. If a conflict involves harm or safety, ask a pastor or a professional for help. As peacemakers multiply, God’s system is built up brick by brick, one relationship at a time.
lessons.light: Forming factions is an extension of the self-centered life: I don’t just want to win; I want to pull a crowd over to my side. The selfless know they are only servants, not masters, and the glory goes to God who gives the growth. We build God’s system not by making one faction stronger, but by all working together with God, building one another up in the same field and the same house.
think: In 1 Corinthians 3:3-9, how does Paul deal with the “I follow so-and-so” quarrels?
Have I recently been pulled into taking sides—or been pulling others to my side?
How will I share “Don’t take sides—build together” with my small group or family this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that in conflict I sometimes pull people to my side, and I am often drawn into other people’s camps. Help me remember that we are all your fellow workers—your field and your building. Make me someone who brings people back to you rather than someone who expands a faction. All glory belongs to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, when someone complains to you about a third person, listen first, then invite them to pray for that person with you. Also share what you’ve learned this week with your small group or family, and agree together: “When we disagree, we bring it to the Lord; we don’t recruit people to take sides.”
lessons.quick: No sides, no factions—we are all God’s fellow workers.
text: for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?
For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” aren’t you fleshly?
Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him?
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.
Now he who plants and he who waters are the same, but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building.

weeks.keyText: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?

weeks.title: First Be Reconciled
weeks.theme: In God’s eyes reconciliation comes before sacrifice—the one who speaks first is not the loser but the one most like the Father.
group: Read Matthew 5:23-24. Why does Jesus tell us to leave our gift at the altar and go be reconciled first?
Is there a “cold-war wall” between you and someone? What keeps you from being the first to speak?
Toward whom are you willing to take the first step of reconciliation this week, and what concrete action will you take?
weeks.sunday: Invite someone you have had friction with—but with whom it is safe to spend time—for a cup of tea or a walk. If meeting in person is too hard, start with a simple message. Before you go, pray for them and ask the Lord to help you listen before you speak. Don’t rush to settle old accounts; simply let them sense that you want to draw near. Afterward, whatever the outcome, thank God for the step you took.

lessons.title: Leave Your Gift at the Altar
lessons.hear:
Picture the scene. A man leads a lamb to the temple, waits in a long line, and finally reaches the altar. Just as the priest reaches out to take his offering, he suddenly remembers: the neighbor at the edge of the village—the one he argued with over a property line—still turns his face away whenever they pass. What should he do? Jesus says, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24).

In its day this was almost shocking. Offering sacrifice was the holiest moment of worship, yet Jesus says: stop first. Not because worship doesn’t matter, but because God takes no pleasure in a gift carried out of a broken relationship. John says it even more bluntly: “he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20). The vertical beam and the horizontal beam of the cross are nailed together.

Notice a detail. Jesus says, “remember that your brother has anything against you” (Matthew 5:23)—not that you have something against him. In other words, even if you feel the fault isn’t all yours, even if you think you are the one who was wronged, the Lord still hands the first step to you. He isn’t asking you to take all the blame; he is asking you to lay down the pride that says, “Whoever speaks first loses.” In the arithmetic of the kingdom, the one who speaks first is not the loser but the one most like the Father.

These words sit inside Jesus’ teaching on “You shall not murder.” Jesus takes the anger and contemptuous names we shrug off with deadly seriousness, because each of them quietly “deletes” a person in our hearts. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: in my group chats, my extended family, my workplace, or my church, is there someone I have quietly deleted? Reconciliation doesn’t have to be finished today. But the gift can be set down, and your feet can turn toward that person.
lessons.light: The self-centered wait for the other person to give in first, because saving face matters more than the relationship. The selfless take the first step, because people matter more than issues and relationships matter more than winning. The order of relationships is God first, then people—yet Jesus shows us that a breach with others can block our worship of God. To let Jesus reign is to let him decide who speaks first.
think: In Matthew 5:21-24, why does Jesus connect anger, insults, and offering sacrifice?
Is there someone I have quietly “deleted” from my heart, and what makes me unwilling to speak first?
What small thing can I do today to turn my steps toward that person?
lessons.speak: Father, while I was still your enemy, you sent your beloved Son to reconcile me to yourself. I confess that I often wait for others to give in first, and I value my pride more than my brother or sister. Shine your light on the people I have deleted from my heart. Give me the courage of a selfless life to leave my gift at the altar and walk toward them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take five quiet minutes today. Write down the name of someone you have friction with and pray one specific blessing over them. If the relationship is safe, send them a simple greeting—without bringing up the past.
lessons.quick: The one who speaks first is not the loser but the one most like the Father.
text: “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Agree with your adversary quickly while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison.
Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there until you have paid the last penny.

lessons.title: A Cold War Is Not Peace
lessons.hear:
In her family group chat, a woman got into an argument with her sister-in-law over who should do what in caring for their aging mother. One line—“You live closer, so of course you should do more”—was met with another: “Then why don’t you just pay for it?” She left the group in anger, and from then on the two families sat at separate tables at her mother’s birthday dinners. She told her small group, “I didn’t yell at anyone. I just stopped talking to her. If we don’t talk, we can’t fight, right?”

It’s a familiar old mindset: a cold war is peace; no fighting means no problem. But a cold war simply moves the fire from the living room to the basement. You can’t see the smoke, yet the foundation keeps burning. Solomon said it long ago: “A brother offended is more difficult than a fortified city” (Proverbs 18:19). Time does not melt the ice on its own; it only makes the walls thicker.

Paul gives us God’s perspective: “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). The sentence has two halves. “If it is possible” is honest: peace takes two, and some people aren’t willing yet. In some situations—where there is violence, threats, or ongoing harm—you need to protect yourself first, and God does not ask you to put yourself in danger. But “as much as it is up to you” leaves no escape hatch: on my side, I must do everything I can. Paul goes on: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). A cold war is really a form of revenge, just a quieter one. Overcoming evil with good is the Lord’s way.

Later, as she prayed, the Spirit showed her something: she wasn’t only angry about her sister-in-law’s words; she was hurt that her own hard work had gone unseen. She rejoined the group and sent her sister-in-law a private message: “Thank you for taking Mom to her follow-up appointment last weekend. I know you’re tired too.” A day later the reply came—just a sticker. The ice didn’t melt overnight, but light was already slipping through the crack in the door.
