lessons.light: A cold war is a quiet form of the self-centered life: no shouting on the surface, but inside we are waiting for the other person to admit defeat. The selfless don’t need to prove they’re right before doing good first; they leave vengeance to God (see Romans 12:19) and keep doing good for themselves. “If it is possible” lets us admit our limits; “as much as it is up to you” keeps us from making excuses.
think: In Romans 12:17-21, what does Paul tell us not to do, and what does he tell us to do?
Have I been treating a cold war—the silent treatment—as if it were peace?
Within what is “up to me,” what is one good thing I can do today?
lessons.speak: Father, forgive me for mistaking coldness for peace and using silence as revenge. Thank you that you know my limits and don’t ask me to be reckless in danger. But in what is up to me, help me do all I can—not to be overcome by evil, but to overcome evil with good. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone you are in a cold war with. Today, find one thing they have done well recently and send them a sincere word of thanks or affirmation—with no “but” attached.
lessons.quick: A cold war is not peace—it just moves the fire to the basement.
text: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.”
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

lessons.title: When You Stand Praying
lessons.hear:
Many people want to reconcile but get stuck on one question: “I’m still angry—how can I go?” Jesus’ answer is surprising. He brings reconciliation into prayer: “Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone; so that your Father, who is in heaven, may also forgive you your transgressions” (Mark 11:25).

This verse comes right after Jesus speaks of mountain-moving faith. It is as if he is saying: Do you want to see mountains move? Sometimes the biggest mountain isn’t outside the city but inside your heart—the resentment you can’t let go. Faith is not only asking God for great things; it is also trusting that God can accomplish in my heart the forgiveness I can’t manage on my own. Forgiveness happens first before God, and only then before people.

Today’s practice has three steps. First, say it out loud in prayer: “Lord, this is how they hurt me. I hand this debt over to you.” Forgiveness isn’t pretending nothing happened; it is no longer trying to collect the debt yourself. Second, choose a fitting way to draw near: a private message, a phone call, a cup of coffee. Pick a time and place where the other person feels safe—not in a group chat or in front of others. Third, when you speak, start with your own part: “I was too harsh that day. I’m sorry.” Don’t open by passing judgment on their wrongs. The door to reconciliation usually opens from our own side first.

If the other person doesn’t respond right away, don’t lose heart, and don’t keep chasing them. You have already left your gift at the altar; what follows is God’s work. But if the relationship involves violence, threats, or ongoing manipulation, reaching out is not today’s assignment. Find a trusted pastor or professional to walk with you first. Safety always comes first.
lessons.light: Forgiveness is where “Serve” begins: loving by the Lord’s life rather than by our own emotions. The Holy Spirit is my guide; he will prompt you when to speak and what to say. Lean on the Spirit with your heart instead of calculating wins and losses with your head—the more you calculate, the more resentful you become.
think: What do I learn from the way Mark 11:22-26 connects faith, prayer, and forgiveness?
What is the “mountain I can’t let go of” in my heart, and am I truly willing to hand it to God?
When I seek reconciliation, what part of it can I say “I’m sorry” for first?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the cross you prayed for the very people who nailed you there. There is a mountain in my heart—a resentment I can’t move on my own. Right now I hand this debt over to you and stop trying to collect it myself. Holy Spirit, guide me about when to speak and what to say, and help me own my part first. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, first speak your forgiveness of someone in prayer. Then write down the first sentence you want to say to them—starting with your own part—and choose a good moment to say it by private message or phone call.
lessons.quick: The biggest mountain is often the resentment we can’t let go.
text: Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God.

For most certainly I tell you, whoever may tell this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ and doesn’t doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says is happening, he shall have whatever he says.
Therefore I tell you, all things whatever you pray and ask for, believe that you have received them, and you shall have them.
Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone; so that your Father, who is in heaven, may also forgive you your transgressions.
But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your transgressions.”

lessons.title: A Reconciliation with Only a Kiss
lessons.hear:
The story of David and his son Absalom is one of Scripture’s most heartbreaking failures of reconciliation. After killing Amnon, Absalom fled and lived in exile for three years. David allowed him back to Jerusalem, but with a strange order: “Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face” (2 Samuel 14:24). So “Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, and he didn’t see the king’s face” (2 Samuel 14:28).

They lived in the same city, yet a wall stood between their hearts. Two years later, Absalom set Joab’s field on fire just to force a meeting. The text says “the king kissed Absalom” (2 Samuel 14:33), but we don’t find a single word of conversation: no confession, no forgiveness, no facing the wound together. That kiss was like a stamp on a form—the paperwork was done, but the heart never came home. Before long Absalom was sitting at the city gate, and “Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel” (2 Samuel 15:6). In the end he raised a rebellion.

This story exposes our own “half reconciliations.” We still sit at the same table for holiday dinners but make sure we aren’t seated together. We still “like” each other’s posts in the group chat but never speak privately. We say, “Let bygones be bygones,” while still keeping score inside. This kind of reconciliation looks mature, but it only seals the problem away. A sealed wound doesn’t heal; it festers in the dark.

Today, review honestly: Have I said, “You may come back, but I won’t see your face”? Have I substituted politeness for sincerity, or used busyness to postpone the conversation that needs to happen? The way to adjust isn’t complicated: move from formality to reality, from a kiss to a conversation. David’s failure also reminds us that our heavenly Father is not that kind of father. He doesn’t leave the prodigal waiting in the city for two years; he is the one who sees him from far off and runs to meet him. Because we have been welcomed like that, we can learn to welcome others the same way.
lessons.light: Self-centered reconciliation only wants things to look good so we don’t have to feel awkward anymore. Selfless reconciliation is willing to pay the price of facing the truth. The 920 reminds us that every “2”—every person connected to us—deserves a real conversation, not just a polite stamp.
think: In 2 Samuel 14:24-33, what elements of reconciliation are missing between David and Absalom?
Do I have a relationship that has been reduced to mere politeness, and what am I avoiding?
What can I do next to move this relationship from formality to reality?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you did not forgive me and then refuse to see me—you embraced me yourself and sat at the table with me. I confess that I often give people half a reconciliation: polite on the outside, keeping score on the inside. Give me courage to bring sealed wounds into the light and to have a real conversation with that brother or sister. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Look at one relationship that is only “reconciled on the surface.” Today, ask that person for a quiet time to talk (in person or by phone), and say honestly, “I’d like to really talk with you about what happened last time.”
lessons.quick: A kiss can stamp the paperwork; only a conversation can heal the wound.
text: Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, and he didn’t see the king’s face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but he would not come to him. Then he sent again a second time, but he would not come.
Therefore he said to his servants, “Behold, Joab’s field is near mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire.” So Absalom’s servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab arose and came to Absalom to his house, and said to him, “Why have your servants set my field on fire?”

Absalom answered Joab, “Behold, I sent to you, saying, ‘Come here, that I may send you to the king, to say, “Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still. Now therefore, let me see the king’s face; and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.”’”
So Joab came to the king and told him; and when he had called for Absalom, he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king; and the king kissed Absalom.

lessons.title: Helping Two People Agree
lessons.hear:
Two women in the church at Philippi were at odds: Euodia and Syntyche. They weren’t on the fringes of the church; they were co-workers who “labored with me in the Good News” (Philippians 4:3), as Paul put it. Paul didn’t pretend nothing was wrong, nor did he publicly rule on who was right. He wrote: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). Then he asked a “true partner” to help them.

This passage gives us two lessons. First, even co-workers who love the Lord can clash. That is no disgrace; the disgrace is letting the conflict spread. The basis of reconciliation is not agreeing on everything but being “in the Lord”—we may see things differently and still bow together before the same Lord. Second, sometimes two people can’t find their way out alone; they need a third person both of them trust to walk alongside them. That third person isn’t a referee or a messenger, but a bridge.

This week we have seen that reconciliation comes before sacrifice; a cold war is not peace; forgiveness begins in prayer; and half reconciliations must move toward the real thing. Now repeat it: each night before bed, ask yourself whether any new knot has formed in your heart today. “Be angry, and don’t sin.” “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath” (Ephesians 4:26). Then multiply it: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Perhaps two friends or two branches of your family near you are in a cold war right now. You don’t have to solve their problem, but you can pray for them, and at the right time gently say, “You’re both precious to me. I’d be glad to sit with you and talk it through.”

Keep a sense of proportion, too: don’t pass one person’s words along to the other, and don’t discuss other people’s conflicts in group chats. Ambassadors of reconciliation keep their mouths tighter than their ears.
lessons.light: Making peace walks the step of “God” on the Way of Service: all glory goes to God, because only he can make two hearts one. The 235 reminds us that spiritual companions don’t just rejoice together—they hold each other up and serve as bridges in times of conflict. First be reconciled yourself, then help others be reconciled. Change begins with me, and then it multiplies.
think: In Philippians 4:2-3, how does Paul handle the conflict between two co-workers?
In other people’s conflicts, do I usually play the bridge, the referee, or the messenger?
Which two people in a cold war can I pray for or walk alongside?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you broke down the dividing wall and made us one in peace. First guard my heart so I don’t let the sun go down on my anger, and then make me a peacemaker. I pray for the two friends near me who are in a cold war: help them think the same way in the Lord, and give me wisdom to know when to speak and when to keep quiet. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight before bed, review whether any new knot has formed in your heart today and hand it to the Lord. Then pray by name for a pair of friends or relatives you know are in a cold war—without repeating what you’ve heard or passing judgment.
lessons.quick: Ambassadors of reconciliation keep their mouths tighter than their ears.
text: I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.
Yes, I beg you also, true partner, help these women, for they labored with me in the Good News with Clement also, and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.

weeks.keyText: leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

weeks.title: Point Out, Listen, Win Back
weeks.theme: When someone wrongs us, the goal is not to win the argument but to win back our brother—privately, gently, and with restoration in view.
group: Read Matthew 18:15. What does Jesus say is the goal of dealing with an offense, and why “between you and him alone”?
When you are wronged, do you tend to complain behind people’s backs, explode in public, or quietly swallow it—and why?
With whom are you willing to talk privately and gently this week about something on your heart, and how do you plan to begin?
weeks.sunday: Go for a walk or a coffee with a spiritual companion you trust, and ask each other one question: “What blind spots do you think I have lately?” Pray first for humble ears. Only listen—don’t defend yourself—and end by saying thank you. When you get home, bring one thing you heard before God and thank him for these “wounds of a friend.”

lessons.title: Between You and Him Alone
lessons.hear:
When someone wrongs us, we usually feel three urges: vent to someone else, demand justice in public, or simply drift away for good. Jesus points to a fourth way: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15).

First, notice where these words sit. Just before them is the parable of the lost sheep: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one that wandered off (see Matthew 18:12-14). Just after them, Peter asks how many times he must forgive. In other words, Jesus’ teaching on pointing out a fault is sandwiched between seeking and forgiving. The goal is not to win a debate but to have “gained back your brother.” If, before I go, I’m thinking about how to make him admit defeat, I’m not ready to go yet.

“Between you and him alone” is an act of respect: it lets the other person save face and leaves room for the matter to be resolved. Many misunderstandings dissolve in a single private conversation, because we had only heard half the story. If he won’t listen, then bring one or two mature, fair-minded people along; only if that fails do we take it to the church. Each step widens the circle of love, not the circle of shame. As for small, harmless frictions, Scripture also says “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Not everything needs a conversation.

But one thing must be made clear: this teaching is for ordinary offenses between brothers and sisters. If the situation involves violence, intimidation, sexual harassment, stalking, or the abuse of power by a boss, an elder, or a spiritual leader, then “go to him privately first” does not apply. Safety comes first. Don’t face it alone. Go first to a trusted third party or an appropriate leader in the church, and when necessary seek help from the police or professionals. This isn’t unspiritual; it is God’s heart to protect the wounded.
lessons.light: Wanting to win is the self-centered life: proving I’m right and you’re wrong. Wanting to win back is the selfless life: setting aside my pride in order to gain my brother. Keep your eyes on Jesus—not on the other person’s fault or on your own hurt. “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” (Matthew 18:20). Even in that hard conversation, the Lord is present.
think: In Matthew 18:15-17, what is the purpose of each step, and why does the order move from private to public?
When I am wronged, is the first person I want to tell the one who wronged me, or someone else?
Is there something I could simply cover with love and never raise again, and what matters do need a conversation?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the Good Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one. Put your heart within me, so that when I am wronged I don’t want to win but to gain back my brother. Give me wisdom to discern what to cover with love and what to speak about privately and gently—and if there is danger, help me know how to seek protection. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one offense you can’t stop thinking about. In prayer, discern: is this something to “cover with love,” or something to “talk about privately”? If it’s the latter, pray for the other person for three days before setting a time to meet.
lessons.quick: The goal of pointing out a fault is not to win the point but to win back your brother.
text: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.
Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven.
Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”

lessons.title: Open Rebuke Beats Hidden Love
lessons.hear:
A man working at a tech company discovered, twice in a row, that a teammate had taken his reports to their manager and claimed the credit. He said nothing to the teammate. Instead he complained to another colleague over lunch and vented to his friends’ group chat after work. Six months later the whole department “knew” that guy steals credit—everyone except the man himself. When the two met in the break room they were perfectly polite, yet their hearts drifted further and further apart.

Behind this lies an old mindset: saying it to someone’s face hurts the relationship too much; saying it behind their back is safer; keeping quiet is patience, and patience is love. But Proverbs turns that mindset upside down: “Better is open rebuke than hidden love. The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse” (Proverbs 27:5-6). God’s view is this: real love sometimes makes people uncomfortable for a moment; false peace keeps them in the dark indefinitely.

Talking behind someone’s back looks gentle, but it actually does more harm. It gives the other person no chance to explain and no chance to change. It turns something between two people into a trial before a crowd. Scripture says, “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down” (Proverbs 26:20). Every retelling throws another log on the fire. The law of Moses even says, “You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him” (Leviticus 19:17). Sometimes not speaking isn’t love at all; it just lets hatred slowly ferment in the heart.

Eventually his small group leader nudged him, and he decided to invite his colleague to talk privately. He didn’t accuse; he simply said, “I stayed up late working on those last two reports. Our manager doesn’t know that, and it’s been weighing on me.” The colleague froze for a moment, then, red-faced, admitted he had been too eager to impress. That day the man didn’t win anything—but he won back a colleague.
lessons.light: Talking behind someone’s back is the self-centered life protecting itself: afraid of conflict and of being disliked, it pays the price with the other person’s reputation. Speaking gently face to face is the courage of the selfless life: willing to bear the awkwardness for the other person’s good. People matter more than issues—and more than my pride.
think: In Proverbs 27:5-6, what kinds of relationships do “wounds” and “kisses” represent?
Have I recently talked about someone behind their back without ever saying it to them directly?
In that situation, can I stop adding wood to the fire and talk with them privately instead?
lessons.speak: Father, forgive me for so often telling everyone what’s on my heart except the one person I should tell. I confess it comes from fearing conflict and loving my pride. Cleanse my mouth and stop my gossip. Give me courage that is both gentle and honest, so that the wounds I give are the faithful wounds of a friend. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, if someone complains to you about a third person, gently ask, “Have you talked to them directly?” And stop passing along one story about someone else yourself.
lessons.quick: Talking behind someone’s back adds wood to the fire; speaking gently face to face puts it out.
text: Better is open rebuke than hidden love.
The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

lessons.title: They Took Him Aside
lessons.hear:
Apollos was a dazzling preacher—“an eloquent man… He was mighty in the Scriptures” (Acts 18:24)—and “fervent in spirit.” But he had a blind spot: “he knew only the baptism of John” (Acts 18:25). A tentmaking couple, Priscilla and Aquila, heard him in the synagogue. They didn’t stand up and correct him on the spot, nor did they stand by the door afterward telling people, “His teaching is incomplete.” The text simply says: “they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26).

That one short sentence is the most beautiful model of how to point something out. First, they listened all the way through: they saw Apollos’s zeal as well as what he lacked, rather than jumping in halfway. Then they “took him aside”—quite likely into their home, around a warm table, talking privately so that he felt welcomed rather than judged. Most important, they didn’t tear him down; they “explained… more accurately.” They affirmed what was right and then supplied the missing piece. Paul tells us to be “speaking truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). Love is the wrapping and truth is the content; neither can be left out.

After that conversation they didn’t simply exit the story. When Apollos wanted to go on to Achaia, “the brothers encouraged him; and wrote to the disciples to receive him.” And when he arrived, “he greatly helped those who had believed through grace” (Acts 18:27). One gentle, private conversation equipped a servant to be even more useful.

Today, think of someone in whom you see a blind spot, or who has done something that hurt you. Perhaps it’s an older relative who keeps forwarding false information in the family chat, or a small group member who wounds people with his words without realizing it. Learn from Priscilla and Aquila: invite them for coffee, start by telling them what you appreciate about them, and then specifically fill in the piece you see missing. If the matter involves violence, harassment, or abuse of power, don’t go alone; first find someone trustworthy or seek professional help.
lessons.light: Priscilla and Aquila didn’t show off how much more they knew in front of others—that is selflessness. They were willing to open their home and spend time filling in what someone else lacked—that is self-denial. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on who is right: the goal is for the other person to know the Lord more fully and serve him better. Here the “9” of the 920 bears the fruit of gentleness and goodness.
think: In Acts 18:24-28, how did Priscilla and Aquila help Apollos?
When I correct someone, do I usually do it in public, or do I welcome them privately and fill in what’s missing?
Whom will I invite to talk privately today, and what will I affirm in them first?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that you so often use other people’s hospitality and reminders to explain your way to me more accurately. Help me learn from Priscilla and Aquila—not to show myself off in front of others, but to open my home and gently fill in what others lack. Give me wisdom and fitting words so that the other person is built up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask someone you want to encourage toward change for coffee or a phone call. First name one specific thing you appreciate about them, then gently add the piece you see missing. You can use the app’s Reconciliation Guide to prepare your opening sentence.
lessons.quick: Listen fully, take them aside, fill in the gap—then send them on with a blessing.
text: Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him; and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace;
for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.

lessons.title: You Are the Man
lessons.hear:
David committed adultery and murder, and then for a long stretch sat on his throne as if nothing had happened. God sent the prophet Nathan to him. Nathan didn’t storm into the palace shouting accusations. Instead he told a story: a rich man with many flocks and herds took a poor man’s only little ewe lamb. David burned with anger and declared that the man who did this deserved to die. Nathan looked at him and said just one thing: “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7).

We can review ourselves from two angles in this scene. First, look at Nathan. He had courage—he dared to speak to a king. He also had wisdom—he used a story to let David first see how ugly the sin was, and only then see himself in it. He didn’t go to vent his frustration; he went because God sent him, for the sake of David’s soul. When we point out someone else’s fault, do we first ask God to send us? Or do we go simply because we can’t hold it in any longer?

Then look at David. He was the king; he could have thrown Nathan out or even had him killed. Instead David said only, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan answered at once, “The LORD also has put away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13). It was the lowest moment of David’s life—and the starting point of his restoration. When someone points out your fault, what is your first reaction? Explaining? Counterattacking? Digging up the other person’s record? Or saying, “You’re right. I was wrong”?

Jesus reminds us too: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:5). Today, adjust two things. Before you point out someone else’s fault, let God point out yours. And when someone points out your fault, don’t rush to defend yourself. Let their words rest in your heart for a while, and ask God, “Is there something here you want to say to me?”
lessons.light: Pride dreads hearing “You are the man,” because it wants to hold on to its throne. Humility can say, “I have sinned against the LORD,” because it is willing to return to its proper place. Humility breeds humility: a person who readily admits their own wrongs is the one best able to help others admit theirs.
think: In 2 Samuel 12:1-13, how did Nathan speak, and how did David respond?
When someone points out my fault, what is my most common reaction?
Which “beam” in my own eye do I need God to remove first today?
lessons.speak: Lord, you sent Nathan to David, and you often send people to me. When I am corrected, help me not to rush to defend myself but to say honestly, “I was wrong.” When I go to correct others, first remove the beam from my own eye. Thank you that your forgiveness is always greater than my failure. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, take the initiative to ask a family member or close friend, “Is there anything I’ve done lately that bothered you?” Only listen—don’t explain—and end by saying, “Thank you for telling me.”
lessons.quick: Those who can say “I was wrong” are best able to help others back onto the right path.
text: The LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him, and said to him, “There were two men in one city: the one rich, and the other poor.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds,

but the poor man had nothing, except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised. It grew up together with him and with his children. It ate of his own food, drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, and he didn’t want to take of his own flock and of his own herd to prepare for the wayfaring man who had come to him, but took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him.”
David’s anger burned hot against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die!
He must restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and because he had no pity!”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.

I gave you your master’s house and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah; and if that would have been too little, I would have added to you many more such things.

Why have you despised the LORD’s word, to do that which is evil in his sight? You have struck Uriah the Hittite with the sword, have taken his wife to be your wife, and have slain him with the sword of the children of Ammon.
Now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken Uriah the Hittite’s wife to be your wife.’

“This is what the LORD says: ‘Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house; and I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.
For you did this secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan said to David, “The LORD also has put away your sin. You will not die.

lessons.title: The Lord’s Servant Must Not Quarrel
lessons.hear:
In the internet age, quarrels are always within reach. Under a single news story, hundreds of comments mock one another; in a family group chat, one forwarded article can spark such a fight that someone leaves the group. When Paul wrote to young Timothy, it was as if he were writing to us today: “But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife. The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all” (2 Timothy 2:23-24).

Notice that Paul doesn’t tell Timothy to stay silent about error. He says the Lord’s servant should be “able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who oppose him” (2 Timothy 2:24-25). The key is the hope at the end: “Perhaps God may give them repentance.” It is God who changes hearts, not my debating skill. My responsibility is to wrap the truth in gentleness and hand it over; when the other person opens it is God’s timing.

This week we have learned the way of Jesus: go privately, with the goal of winning back your brother; speak gently to someone’s face rather than discussing them behind their back; like Priscilla and Aquila, take people aside and fill in what they lack; and when corrected, admit your wrong as David did. Remember again: this path does not apply where there is violence, sexual harassment, or abuse of power. In those cases safety comes first, and you should find a trusted third party.

Now it’s time to repeat and to multiply. To repeat means that the next time you want to fire back in the comments or complain behind someone’s back, you pause for three seconds and ask, “Is this quarreling, or is this winning someone back?” To multiply means bringing this culture into your small group or ministry team: agree together that when there’s friction, you’ll talk privately—no public trials in the group chat and no passing along gossip. A small community willing to make that commitment is like ground that won’t catch fire, and there God’s kingdom takes root.
lessons.light: Quarreling is the battlefield of the self-centered life, where everyone wants to be king. Gentleness is the soil of the selfless life, where we let Jesus reign. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. When a small group learns to speak privately, gently, and with restoration as the goal, God’s system is built into its relationships.
think: In 2 Timothy 2:23-26, what must the Lord’s servant refuse, and how should he treat people?
Where am I most easily drawn into quarrels—online, in my extended family, or at work?
Whom can I invite to make a shared commitment to “talk privately, no public trials”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, when you were insulted you did not insult in return, and you won back my heart with gentleness. Help me refuse foolish arguments and be gentle toward all. Help my small group and ministry team become a community that speaks privately, speaks gently, and aims to restore, so that you reign among us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, share what you have learned with your small group or ministry team, and invite everyone to agree: when there’s friction, talk privately first—no public trials in the group chat and no passing along gossip about others.
lessons.quick: God changes hearts; my job is just to wrap the truth in gentleness.
text: But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,
and they may recover themselves out of the devil’s snare, having been taken captive by him to do his will.

weeks.title: The Art of Apology and Forgiveness
weeks.theme: A true apology makes no excuses and true forgiveness doesn’t dig up the past—the Father’s embrace is the most beautiful picture of reconciliation.
group: Read Luke 15:17-24. What elements make up the younger son’s apology, and how does the father’s response go beyond it?
Is it harder for you to say sorry or to forgive from the heart, and what lies behind that?
This week, to whom will you offer an apology with no “but” attached, or for whom will you let go of an old account?
weeks.sunday: Share a meal with your family or housemates. Before eating, take turns completing the sentence “This week, what I want to say sorry to you for is…” and then add one “thank you.” Pray beforehand that the Lord will keep the atmosphere gentle, with no one keeping score. Families with children can use this as a chance to teach them how to make a complete apology. After the meal, thank God together for the forgiveness you have shared.

lessons.title: The Father Ran and Embraced Him
lessons.hear:
The story of the prodigal son is the most moving reconciliation story Jesus ever told. The younger son took his share of the estate, went far away, squandered everything, and sank so low that he longed to eat the pigs’ pods. The story turns on one phrase: “when he came to himself” (Luke 15:17). There in the pigpen he drafted a speech, and then he got up and headed home.

Look closely at that speech—it is a model of a true apology. First, confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight” (Luke 15:21). No “my older brother was too harsh,” no “my friends out there led me astray,” and no “if you felt hurt.” He confessed wrongdoing, not feelings. Second, no excuses and no bargaining: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” Third, a willingness to bear the consequences: he was ready to say, “Make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:19), prepared to work to make things right.

Yet the real hero of the story isn’t the son but the father. “But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). In that culture, a respected older man hitching up his robe and running through the village was undignified—and the father didn’t care. He didn’t even let his son finish the speech before calling for the robe, the ring, and the sandals. The robe meant honor, the ring meant family authority, and sandals marked a son; hired servants went barefoot.

This is the gospel: before we finish our apology, the Father has already come running. “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). We learn to apologize because we were forgiven first; we learn to forgive because we were embraced first.
lessons.light: The prodigal’s “coming to himself” was a change of mindset: from “I want what’s mine” to “I have sinned against heaven.” Change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your relationships change. The father’s running shows us that selfless love doesn’t care about saving face—it cares only that what was lost has been found.
think: In Luke 15:17-24, what did the son say, and what did the father do?
When I apologize, do I often slip in a “but” or an “if you felt that way”?
How can I pass on the Father’s embrace today to someone who needs to be accepted?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that before I could finish confessing, you ran to embrace me and gave me the robe, the ring, and the sandals. I confess that when I apologize I often make excuses, and when I forgive I still keep score. Fill me with your compassion so that I can apologize sincerely and forgive sincerely. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in prayer, confess one specific sin to God the way the prodigal did—with no excuses. Then quietly receive his forgiveness and write one sentence of thanks for it.
lessons.quick: We learn to apologize and forgive because the Father ran to embrace us first.
text: But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!
I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.
I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.”’
“He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.

lessons.title: Zacchaeus’s Apology Had Weight
lessons.hear:
More than ten years ago, a man borrowed money from his college roommate to start a business. When the business failed, he changed his phone number and avoided every class reunion. After he came to faith, the matter weighed on him constantly. He thought, “It’s all in the past. He’s probably forgotten. Or maybe I could just send a message saying sorry for the trouble.”

This is a common old mindset: an apology means saying “Sorry about that,” or “If I did anything wrong, please forgive me.” Such words sound polite, but they blur responsibility—and sometimes they even hint that the real problem is that you’re too sensitive. God’s perspective shows most clearly in Zacchaeus. Jesus took the initiative and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). Grace arrived first, and Zacchaeus’s heart opened. He stood up and said, “If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much” (Luke 19:8).

Zacchaeus’s apology had weight because it contained three things. Confession: he didn’t say, “Every tax collector does it.” No excuses: he didn’t mention pressure from the Roman government. A willingness to make amends: and beyond what the law required. A true apology isn’t a phrase but a turning around. It lets the person who was hurt see that you truly know what you did and that you truly want to take responsibility.

In the end, that man wrote his roommate a long message: “Years ago I borrowed your money, and after the business failed, I not only didn’t pay you back—I hid from you. That was my fault, and I have no excuse. Starting next month I’d like to repay you in installments, and I’d like to apologize to you in person.” A week passed before the roommate replied: “I thought you had stopped seeing me as a friend long ago.” Over that meal, ten years late, both men wept. He says that after repaying the money, he could attend a reunion with a clear conscience for the first time.
lessons.light: A self-centered apology is meant to make ourselves feel better: say it fast and turn the page. A selfless apology is meant to bring the other person healing: willing to take responsibility and pay the price. Zacchaeus was accepted by Jesus first, and only then did he have the strength to face his own accounts. Grace always goes ahead of repentance.
think: In Luke 19:5-10, who takes the first step, Jesus or Zacchaeus, and why does that matter?
Have my past apologies been missing confession, the refusal to make excuses, or a willingness to make amends?
Is there a debt I owe someone—money, a promise, or respect—that I need to face?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you came to Zacchaeus’s house on your own initiative, and you came into my life the same way. Give me Zacchaeus’s courage to face what I owe others instead of glossing over it. Make my apologies honest in confession, free of excuses, and ready to make amends, so that others can see your salvation in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a situation where you owe someone a complete apology. Today, write three sentences: what I did, the excuse I won’t make, and how I am willing to make it right. Ask the Lord to show you when to say it.
lessons.quick: A true apology = confession + no excuses + willingness to make amends.
text: When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

lessons.title: Meeting Esau with Gifts
lessons.hear:
Jacob had cheated his brother Esau out of his blessing and fled his homeland for twenty years. Now he was going back, and when he heard that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men, he prayed in terror: “for I fear him, lest he come and strike me” (Genesis 32:11). Yet he didn’t turn back; he went forward. The text says: “He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother” (Genesis 33:3).

Jacob used to be the man who hid behind others and won by scheming. This time he went first and bowed low. He also sent a generous gift and called Esau “my lord,” giving back through his actions part of the blessing he had once stolen. This is the action side of an apology: not only saying it, but paying a cost. Then something wonderful happened: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept” (Genesis 33:4). Jacob said, “I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God” (Genesis 33:10).

Today’s practice is to make one true apology. You can use three sentences: “I did… (the specific thing).” “That was my fault; I won’t make excuses.” “How can I make it right?” Then stop. Don’t follow it with “But you also…” An apology is a gift you hand over, not a bargaining chip.

Understand, too, that the other person’s response is not in your hands. Esau’s embrace was grace, not something Jacob earned. Some people will embrace you, some will need time, and some won’t accept it for now; you can respect their pace. It is worth noticing that after the two brothers reconciled, they didn’t travel together but each went his own way (see Genesis 33:12-17). Reconciliation doesn’t always mean returning to the old closeness, and forgiveness doesn’t mean trust is restored immediately. Sometimes a peaceful distance is exactly what wisdom calls for.
lessons.light: Jacob went from a man who grasped to a man who bowed—a change from the self-centered life to the selfless life. Change begins with me: I can’t control whether the other person will embrace me, but I can choose to go first and bow low. Let Jesus reign, and leave the outcome with him.
think: In Genesis 33:1-11, how did Jacob’s attitude and actions differ from twenty years earlier?
Do I treat apologizing like a negotiation, expecting the other person to admit their wrong too?
With which three sentences, and to whom, will I make a true apology today?
lessons.speak: Father, Jacob was afraid of Esau, and I am afraid to face the people I have wronged. Give me courage to go first and bow low, apologizing with concrete words and actions and without conditions. I place their response in your hands; if they need time, help me respect it patiently. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone you have wronged and make an apology in three sentences (what I did / I won’t make excuses / how I am willing to make it right). Then stop, without demanding a response.
lessons.quick: An apology is a gift you hand over, not a bargaining chip.
text: Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants.
He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear.
He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
He lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, “Who are these with you?” He said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.”
Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed themselves.
Leah also and her children came near, and bowed themselves. After them, Joseph came near with Rachel, and they bowed themselves.
Esau said, “What do you mean by all this company which I met?” Jacob said, “To find favor in the sight of my lord.”
Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours.”
Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.
Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it.

lessons.title: The Older Son Who Wouldn’t Go In
lessons.hear:
The prodigal is home and the music is playing, but the story isn’t over. The older son comes in from the fields, hears the music and dancing, and “he was angry and would not go in” (Luke 15:28). Standing outside, he lays out the account he has been keeping for years: “Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat… But when this your son came…” (Luke 15:29-30).

Listen to his words. He doesn’t say “my brother”; he says “this your son.” He lists his brother’s old failures item by item. This is what unforgiveness looks like: a ledger in the heart, recorded in perfect detail and ready to be opened at any moment. Outwardly he was the good son who never left home; inwardly he was far from his father too—he just happened to live under the same roof.

Today, let the older son be a mirror. First, do I use my own “goodness” as a reason not to forgive? “I didn’t do anything wrong—why should he be let off?” Second, do I often dig up the past? In an argument, the words “You always do this” are the sound of the ledger being opened. Third, do I feel a sour twinge when I see others receive grace?

The way to adjust is seen in the father. He came out and pleaded with the older son too: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). The root of unforgiveness is often a sense that we are lacking; only those filled with the Father’s love have room to forgive. Be clear about this as well: forgiveness means no longer demanding repayment and no longer reopening the ledger. It doesn’t mean denying that the hurt happened, nor does it mean you must immediately trust someone who is still hurting others. Trust is rebuilt over time and through actions; forgiveness, though, can begin before God today.
lessons.light: The older son’s problem wasn’t doing wrong but the self-righteousness of the self-centered life: believing he deserved good things and others didn’t. The selfless know they are sinners saved by grace just the same, so they can go inside and celebrate. Forgiveness isn’t losing something; it is laying down the ledger and entering the riches of the Father’s house.
think: In Luke 15:28-32, what accounts had the older son been keeping, and how did the father respond?
Is there a ledger in my heart too, and which page do I open most often?
Which page will I tear out before God today, choosing not to dig up the past again?
lessons.speak: Father, I am often like the older son, standing outside keeping accounts and refusing to come in and celebrate. Forgive my self-righteousness, and thank you for saying, “All that is mine is yours.” Today I hand you my ledger, and I will stop digging up the past. As for trust, give me wisdom to rebuild it slowly, in step with real change. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one old account you keep reopening. In prayer, say, “Lord, I hand this account over to you,” and then tear up the paper. The next time there’s a disagreement, remind yourself not to say, “You always…”
lessons.quick: Forgiveness is laying down the ledger and walking into the Father’s celebration.
text: “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on.
He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’
But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.
But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’
“He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’”

lessons.title: Confirm Your Love Toward Him
lessons.hear:
A man in the Corinthian church had committed a serious wrong, and the church dealt with it as Paul had advised. Later the man repented—but now Paul worried about a different problem: would everyone refuse to let him go? He wrote: “you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him” (2 Corinthians 2:7-8).

These words show us that forgiveness isn’t only a personal matter but a community matter. What a repentant person needs most isn’t a tenth reminder but a seat where he can sit down again. Paul even says that refusing to forgive leaves an opening for Satan (see 2 Corinthians 2:11). Nothing pleases the enemy more than brothers and sisters living inside each other’s ledgers.

This week, from the prodigal and his father, we have seen the whole picture of reconciliation. A true apology confesses, makes no excuses, and is willing to make amends; true forgiveness stops demanding repayment and doesn’t dig up the past. We also drew some distinctions: forgiveness can be given first by one side, but reconciliation takes two; forgiveness doesn’t deny the hurt, nor does it mean trust is restored right away; trust is rebuilt through time and genuine change. Where the hurt involves violence or safety, protecting yourself and others still comes first.

Now repeat it: each night before bed, pray as the Lord’s Prayer says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). Then multiply it: teach the next generation how to make a complete apology. When children fight, don’t just make them say “Sorry.” Teach them to say, “I’m sorry I grabbed your toy. Next time I’ll ask you first.” A home that knows how to apologize well and forgive well is a small picture of the Father’s house.
lessons.light: Spiritual parents in the 235 don’t just teach children to memorize verses; they model how to apologize. When a parent says to a child, “I’m sorry—Dad was too harsh just now,” that is the most powerful multiplication of all. People matter more than issues; an adult who is willing to humble himself raises a generation that knows how to reconcile.
think: In 2 Corinthians 2:5-11, why does Paul urge the church to forgive and comfort the man?
Is there someone around me who has already repented but whom I still “hold on record”?
How can I model or teach a complete apology to someone younger than me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you not only forgive me but comfort me and give me a seat at the table again. Help me confirm my love toward those who repent, and don’t let Satan take the opportunity to build walls among us. Help me model true apology and true forgiveness in my home and small group, and pass them on to the next generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, model a complete apology for someone younger—a child, a younger student, or a new friend—or teach them to apologize using the pattern “I did…; next time I will…”
lessons.quick: A home that can apologize and forgive is a small picture of the Father’s house.
